Because the arising of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) compensates for the habitual cause (*vāsanā-hetu*), it constitutes a fruit of habituation (*vāsanā-phala*). Since untainted phenomena diminish birth and are not dharmas that draw forth birth, there is no subsequent retribution.

As for the three fruits that possess retribution, their residual karmic thoughts (*saṃskāra*) are not yet exhausted; they may undergo seven more births, or one more "coming and going" (*ekābhinivṛtti*).
Alternatively, birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is not an outflow-free retribution (*anāsrava-vipāka*). For this reason, there are only nine [types of birth] and not ten.
According to the Mahāyāna, even this [birth] is still termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). As the Great Sūtra states: "The adornment of merit is conditioned and with outflows.

Since the Śrāvaka Saṃgha is not without outflows and has not eliminated their specific afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), they still undergo the birth of transformation (*nairmāṇika-jāti*). Thus, [in this context], it is considered "without outflows" (*anāsrava*).
Because ignorance serves as the condition for the arising of the *pariṇāma-kṣetra* (transformed land), there is indeed retribution.
Next, regarding the ten dharmas of the Bodhisattva-Buddha realm, these are further subdivided into three types of Bodhisattvas.

First, as for the Bodhisattva of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), taking merit as the cause, their characteristics, nature, power, and virtuous karma constitute the cause, while afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute the condition. Third...
In the case of the Buddha, who attains the fruit by severing the fetters through fourteen minds, there is no retribution; however, the Bodhisattva possesses all ten.

Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), if one discusses them in terms of the untainted (anāsrava), before the sixth stage (*bhūmi*), residual thoughts still receive retribution. At the sixth stage, when thoughts are exhausted, they do not receive a subsequent body;

because they vow to manifest birth by supporting their residual habits rather than through actual karmic retribution, they possess only nine and lack the tenth. As for the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao)...

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s sequential contemplation based on the practice of the Middle Way, ten dharmas are discussed. Although such a person has severed the pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), they know that birth still exists;
thus, they possess these ten dharmas. Now, as for birth through transformation (*pariṇāmika-janman*), there are three different types:

first, those whose distinct afflictions (*viśeṣa-kleśa*) have not been severed at all who undergo birth through transformation—these are the two vehicles of the Tripiṭaka and the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).
First, those like ordinary beings of the *pratisandhi* stage who do not subdue the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);

second, those who subdue the distinct delusions (*bhinna-āvaraṇa*) and give rise to the *nirmāṇa-bhava* (transformation body), namely the practitioners of the thirty minds of the Distinct Teaching (*bhinna-dharma*) who practice the Middle Way and subdue but do not sever [the delusions]—these are comparable to the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*) of the *pratisandhi* Śrāvakas;
third, those who sever the distinct delusions and give rise to the *nirmāṇa-bhava*, such as those on the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Abiding in the severance of delusions is of this same category. For example, although one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has severed the delusions of the truths (*satyadarśana*), they still undergo seven more births;

it is the same for them. If those who have not yet severed or suppressed [the delusions] are born, they take skillful means and the truly untainted (*anāsrava*) as their cause, and ignorance (*avidyā*) as their condition.

If they have suppressed and severed them, they take the craving for the Dharma that accords with the Path (*mārgānulomikadharmatṛṣṇā*) as their cause and ignorance as their condition to be born in the land of transformation (*nirmāṇabhava*).
The ten dharmas of the Buddha-realm are all distinguished in terms of the Middle Way. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"All sentient beings possess the mark of bodhi, which cannot be further acquired. This refers to the fact that the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*) constitute the marks of Buddhahood;
because they are based within, wisdom and vows remain undiminished. Wisdom is the understanding-cause (*jñāna-hetu*), and the self-nature of the pure mind is precisely the Buddha-nature itself.
Because the Buddha-body is precisely these three tracks (*triyāna*). "Power" refers to the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, which surpasses the two vehicles;
this is called power. "Action" refers to the four great vows and the solemn commitment; this is the cause. "Condition" refers to the adornment of merit; this is the condition.
"Fruit" refers to the Great Enlightenment of the single thought-moment of correspondence, wherein the unsurpassed bodhi is brilliantly manifest; this is the practice.

The "fruit of retribution" refers to the Great Parinirvāṇa; as for the "fruit of fruits," it is the perfection of all virtues, meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and samādhis—this is the fruit of retribution.
Regarding "equality of beginning and end": this means that the three truths of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and nature (*svabhāva*) are not different from the ultimate three truths;

hence they are called equal. Regarding "equality of the truth of emptiness": from the original suchness (*tathatā*) of sentient beings up to the suchness of the Buddha, all are equal. This is the conventional [truth].

Regarding "the truths" (*satya*) and so forth: when sentient beings have not yet resolved their minds [on enlightenment], the Buddha grants them the prediction that they shall become Buddhas; once they have already become Buddhas, he speaks of the events of his past lives (*jātaka*).

This refers to the characteristics of the beginning and the end within the conventional (*prajñapti*) and so forth. Regarding "the middle": both ordinary beings and sages are the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Even within the realm of the Buddha, there are nine or ten [stages]; this is spoken in general terms. From each stage (*bhūmi*), there are the myriad practices of merit (*puṇya*).
With virtue as the cause and ignorance as the condition, one attains the ten dharmas of the habitual fruit and the retributive fruit, none of which are incomplete.

This sutra states: "One attains the immeasurable, untainted, and pure fruits of retribution; having long cultivated the holy life within the Dharma of the Dharma-King, it is only today that one finally obtains this retribution.
It further states: "That which is obtained through long-cultivated karma. The Great Sutra says: "I, now..."

Regarding the food offered, may one obtain the unsurpassed retribution. The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in the fruit-retribution. The *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) states:

"Cyclic existence through causes and conditions and cyclic existence subsequent to [birth] are both partial discussions of fruit-retribution. Fruit-retribution is precisely birth and cessation. Why is this?
Because the portion of ignorance is exhausted, it is therefore discussed as cessation; because true illumination increases, it is therefore called birth.
Furthermore, because residual ignorance still remains, it is said that "a portion of delusions arises"; because this [ignorance] is eliminated, it is said that [delusions] are "extinguished.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One person can weed, while another can sow; the myriad practices provide the support for completion, just as sowing provides the seeds.

Wisdom destroys delusions, just as weeding does; the intention behind 'increasing the Path and diminishing the mind of birth' lies herein. In all forty-one stages (*bhūmi*), there are ten factors. If one approaches them from the perspective of the Sublime...

Awakening is both ninefold and tenfold. Why? Because the wisdom of the Middle Way is what eliminates birth; yet since birth has not yet been entirely exhausted, there are differences in the arising and ceasing across the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Since the meaning of eliminating birth is fully realized only at the stage of Subtle Awakening (*sūkṣma-bodhi*), how could retribution be discussed at the very end?
Therefore it is said: "Only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land. When the thirty births are exhausted, one becomes equal to the Great Awakened One, with no further existence of birth and death.

Because afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted, the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is already perfected; there is no longer any fruit of cultivation, as he does not undergo future rebirths, nor is there any fruit of retribution.

Furthermore, regarding the present life and future lives, nine [aspects] and ten [aspects] are discussed. If one follows the text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states, "I vow to obtain the unsurpassed retribution," this clarifies that the retribution within the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu*) is unsurpassed.
Since the Buddha's retribution is said to be unsurpassed, the Buddha’s marks, nature, and so forth—these nine [aspects]—are likewise unsurpassed.
All dharmas are entirely unsurpassed. What is this? The characteristics and nature of the six realms of existence fully manifest the five abodes;

the characteristics and nature of the two vehicles manifest the breaking of the four abodes and fully manifest ignorance; the characteristics and nature of Bodhisattvas manifest the sequential breaking of the five abodes;

and the characteristics and nature of Buddhas manifest the purity of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is like empty space because it is not defiled by the five abodes. Therefore, the ten dharmas of a Buddha are supreme.
It is unsurpassed.
Furthermore, the six realms of existence signify the suffering of birth and death; the two vehicles signify the bliss of nirvana;

and the Buddha-realm signifies the Middle Way—neither birth-and-death nor nirvana—which is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha-realm is the most unsurpassed.

Furthermore, the four paths represent unwholesome [states], the human and celestial realms represent wholesome [states], the two vehicles represent untainted wholesome [states], and Bodhisattvas and Buddhas represent wholesome [states] that are neither tainted nor untainted; therefore, the Buddha-realm is the most supreme.

Furthermore, the six realms represent all phenomena produced by causes and conditions, the two vehicles represent emptiness, Bodhisattvas represent the provisional (upāya), and Buddhas represent both emptiness and the provisional.
Because it is central, the Buddha-realm is the most unsurpassed. Furthermore, the four realms of existence merely manifest evil and cannot manifest good;
the characteristics of humans and devas merely manifest good and cannot manifest evil; the two vehicles merely manifest the outflow-free (anāsrava) and do not encompass both good and evil.

The characteristics of the Buddha, however, encompass and manifest all characteristics. If one understands the characteristics of the Buddha, one immediately understands all characteristics. Therefore:
The Buddha-realm is the most supreme. If one employs this Dharma to traverse the teachings of the five flavors:

in the Milk Teaching, it is said that the natures and characteristics of both the Bodhisattva-realm and the Buddha-realm may involve entering the provisional (the conventional) or entering the middle;

entering the middle is indeed supreme, yet it still carries a single expedient and is not yet fully supreme. In the Curd Teaching, only the natures and characteristics of the Two Vehicles are clarified.

If one does not even clearly understand entering into the analysis of emptiness (*vibhajya-śūnyatā*) and so forth, let alone entering into immediate emptiness (*sākṣāt-śūnyatā*) and the rest, how much less could one understand the others?

Therefore, this is not the supreme *mantha* (curd). Regarding the four kinds of characteristics of nature (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*): some enter through the analysis of emptiness, some enter through immediate emptiness, some enter through immediate conventionality (*prajñapti*), and some enter through immediate centrality (*madhyama*).
Only the Buddha’s characteristics of nature can enter into the state where they are simultaneously empty, conventional, and central, while still retaining [their distinct qualities].
Because it employs three skillful means, it is not supreme. Regarding the clarification of the three types of *dharmatā* (nature):

one may enter directly into emptiness, or enter directly into the provisional, or enter directly into the Middle Way. Only the *dharmatā* of the Buddhas can enter directly into emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle Way;
however, because this [other teaching] still carries two skillful means, it is not supreme. This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that all nine types of *dharmatā* enter directly into emptiness.

The provisional is identical to the middle; you are truly my son, and I am truly your father. All things are of one color and one flavor, being purely the Buddha-dharma with no other dharma whatsoever.
Thus, one knows that the Buddha-realm is the most unsurpassed.

Furthermore, while the nine aspects (navanimitta) explained in other sutras do not allow entry into the nature of the Buddha’s aspects—which are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle—this sutra opens up all skillful means so that all may universally enter them.
Moreover, these very aspects are themselves simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle;
it does not merely involve leading others into them. For this reason, the Tathāgata earnestly praises this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The Sūtras are the most unsurpassed; this is their intended meaning. Furthermore, although the hundred realms and thousand phenomena are vast and manifold, they are synthesized through the Sūtras and Śāstras so that they may be easily understood.
As a verse in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty;

they are also designated as provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. The characteristics and natures of the six realms of existence are precisely these causes and conditions.
The dharmas that arise—namely, the characteristics and natures of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), which I have taught as being emptiness;

the characteristics and natures of the bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao) of the Six Perfections, which are also called provisional names; and the characteristics and natures of the Buddha-realm, which are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
To summarize the essential points: although this is brief, it encompasses the many meanings mentioned previously, which can thus be seen. Furthermore, there is a verse from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:

It is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing. Once arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) is bliss.

The characteristics and nature of the six realms of existence are precisely these conditioned phenomena. The characteristics and nature of the Two Vehicles according to the Shared Teaching are impermanence.

The characteristics and nature of the Bodhisattvas according to the Distinct Teaching are the cessation of arising and ceasing. The characteristics and nature of the Buddha-realm are quiescent extinction as bliss. Furthermore, there is arising and ceasing...

That "extinguishing is quiescence, which is bliss" refers to the characteristics and nature of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), wherein even within arising and ceasing there is still quiescence;
it does not wait until after extinction has occurred to be called bliss. This is the characteristics and nature of the Buddha-realm according to the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*).
Furthermore, the Universal Precept Verse of the Seven Buddhas says: "Commit no evil, practice all good, and purify one's own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas. (4)
The nature of the destinies is the nature of all evil beings; the nature of devas and humans is the nature of all virtues.

To purify one’s own mind is the nature of the analytical realization of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). To enter the conventional with a purified mind is the nature of a bodhisattva.

To enter the Middle Way with a purified mind is the nature of the Buddha-realm. If one can understand these ten natures and harmonize them with the various sūtras, śāstras, and vinayas, [one attains liberation].

Reaching old age and death is likewise due to the lack of awakening through delusion (*moha*). Because one does not awaken to delusion at its inception, one remains unawakened to it until reaching old age and death.
Delusion gives rise to birth, and because of delusion there is death. If one can awaken to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), then dependent origination will no longer function.
Because delusion does not function, old age and death in the future are exhausted; this is called wisdom (*prajñā*), and wisdom follows the Path.

Second, regarding the twelve [links] being neither produced nor extinguished through skillful means: the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states that for disciples of sharp faculties, it is taught that the twelve [links] are neither produced nor extinguished.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is like space, up to and including old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which are like space;

because ignorance is like an illusion or a magical transformation and is unapprehendable, up to and including old age and death, they are like illusions or magical transformations and are unapprehendable.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that the essence and characteristics of ignorance (*avidyā*) are fundamentally non-existent;

it exists only through the combination of delusive causes and conditions, produced by the mental formations of unwholesome thoughts. It is like a magician at a crossroads who conjures various elephants, horses, necklaces, and human figures;
the ignorant take these to be real, while the wise know they are not true. Thus, ignorance produces the six realms of existence as an illusion.
Based on this correct principle, one should know that [the twelve links] are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning, being merely the products of ignorance.

Just as knowing that the vine is not a snake causes the mind of fear to cease, so too, because they do not arise, they do not cease; this is called the characteristic of the twelve links of dependent origination as neither-arising-nor-ceasing through conceptual investigation.

Regarding the third [point], the inconceivable causes and conditions of arising and ceasing: this refers to the teaching on the dharmas outside the realms (*dhātu*), which breaks down the small and expands the great, explained for the two types of conditions—the sharp and the dull.
The *Avataṃsaka* states: "The mind is like a skilled painter; it creates the various five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Within all worlds, there is nothing that is not constructed from the mind. This "painter" is precisely the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*), and "all worlds" refers to the ten [realms].

The Dharma-realm, whether provisional or substantial, and the lands and so forth, as well as the mind of ignorance—whether self-arisen, other-arisen, co-arisen, or causeless—all four propositions are inconceivable.
However, if there are conditions for the four *siddhāntas*, they may also be explained.

Just as one cannot find a dream through the four propositions, yet speaks of seeing all manner of things within a dream, so too one seeks ignorance through the four propositions [and finds it inconceivable].

It cannot be apprehended; yet from ignorance there arise all phenomena within and without the realm. Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination within the realm, they have been explained as before.
As for the twelve links of dependent origination outside the realm, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:

"The wisdom of emptiness of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas has never seen the body of the Tathāgata. Although the two vehicles possess the four pairs of opposites such as impermanence and so forth, [they do not perceive it].

The treatment of that which relies upon the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is further a perversion; because it is a perversion, it is precisely the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*). Within this untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), there are four kinds of hindrances:

namely, the conditions, the characteristics, the production, and the destruction of conditions. Regarding "conditions" (*pratyaya*): it refers to the abiding ground of ignorance acting as the condition for formative forces (*saṃskāra*). Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*):

it refers to the fact that ignorance and formative forces act together as causes. Regarding "production" (*utpāda*): it refers to the abiding ground of ignorance acting together with [formative forces]...

The cause of the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) is untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*). Their destruction refers to the inconceivable death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) associated with these three kinds of mind-made bodies.
This is analogous to the twelve links of dependent origination within the realms, which proceed from ignorance (*avidyā*) to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

Here, "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the link of ignorance; "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); and "birth" (*janman*) refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the subsequent links.

The five branches [of the *kleśa-skandha*] are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*); the three branches can be understood by analogy with what precedes. "Destruction" (*bhaṅga*) refers to the branches of birth-and-death (*jāti-jarāmaraṇa*).
Although these twelve branches are numerically identical to those within the [three] realms, their underlying meaning is vastly different. That treatise states:

"The three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) have not yet attained liberation from the defilement of ignorance (*avidyā-mala*), nor have they attained ultimate unconditioned purity (*anāsrava-viśuddhi*); the subtle conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of ignorance has not been eternally extinguished."

Having attained the ultimate unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet because the causes for the accumulation of subtle conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)—namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and out-flow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*)—have not been permanently extinguished, the aggregate of mind (*nāma-skandha*) has not yet ceased;

because ultimate unconditioned bliss has not been attained, the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*) have not been completely extinguished;
and because the ultimate nectar (*amṛta*) has not been realized, one does not attain great purity due to the path of conditioned afflictions and the characteristics of karma.
Because of the path of birth, one cannot attain the eight masteries; because of the path of suffering, one cannot attain great bliss;

and because of the destruction of old age and death, one cannot attain the immutable constant. This is the characteristic of the inconceivable arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination outside the realms.
The four inconceivables and the non-arising, non-ceasing twelvefold dependent origination are the manifestation of principle through phenomena for those of sharp faculties.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "The twelvefold dependent origination is called Buddha-nature.
Since ignorance, craving, and grasping are afflictions, and the path of affliction is itself bodhi, when bodhi is thoroughly realized, there are no further afflictions. When afflictions are absent...
That which is the ultimate, pure cause of realization is the Buddha-nature of the *yāna* (path). That which is the path of action (*karmapatha*) is liberation;
this is the Buddha-nature of the condition for liberation and mastery. Name-and-form, old age, and death constitute the path of suffering; suffering is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Dharma-body is neither suffering nor pleasure—it is called Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). It is neither born nor does it die—it is the eternal, primary cause of the Buddha-nature. Therefore...
It is said that between ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) lies the Middle Way. Ignorance belongs to the past and craving belongs to the present;
whether at the extremes or in the middle, there is nothing that is not Buddha-nature. All are eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
That ignorance neither arises nor ceases is called the inconceivable non-arising and non-ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination.

Second, regarding the judgment of the coarse and the subtle: the objects of the causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya) are not inherently coarse or subtle; rather, differences in rank arise from the shallowness or depth of one's apprehension of them.
The first three are provisional and thus coarse, while the last one is real and thus subtle; this can be understood by examining the five flavors.
Third, regarding the revelation [of the true nature]: as the Sūtra states, "My Dharma is subtle and inconceivable.

Since the preceding three [categories] are all Buddha-dharmas, how could there be a coarse difference between what is conceivable and the inconceivable wonder? It is simply that the essence of the conceivable is itself the inconceivable.
When the Tathāgata, through inconceivable skillful means, speaks of the coarse, how can one maintain that the coarse differs from the wonderful?

Fourth, regarding the contemplation of the mind: one contemplates that a single moment of ignorance is itself great enlightenment. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Ignorance and enlightenment are ultimately emptiness.
When the wisdom of emptiness illuminates ignorance, that ignorance is itself purity. It is like a person who, upon perceiving a thief, finds the thief rendered powerless;
since one is no longer defiled by ignorance, this is the purification of the path of afflictions. When afflictions are purified, [the mind is pure].
Therefore, there is no karma; because there is no karma, there is no bondage; because there is no bondage, this is the self-existent Self (*svayambhū ātman*).
Since I am self-existent and not bound by karma, who would experience this name-and-form, contact, sensation, and craving? If there is no craving, there is no suffering.

Since there is no aggregate of suffering, who could undergo transmigration and cessation? This is the nature of permanence. Since the single thought-moment already possesses the twelve links of dependent origination, one should contemplate this.

By means of causes and conditions, one constantly practices the contemplation of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; as the mind dwells moment by moment within the secret treasury, constantly performing this contemplation, it is called "entrusting oneself to the holy embryo.
When the practice matures and the stage of the embryo is perfected, if one breaks through ignorance, it is called "emerging from the holy embryo."

The objects of the Three Clarities (*tisro vidyāḥ*) and the Four Truths (*catvāri satyāni*) constitute four [sections]: first, clarifying the Four Truths; second, judging the coarse and the subtle; third, opening and revealing [the truth]; and fourth, contemplating the mind as the Four Truths. Regarding the Four Truths of contemplating the mind, there are four types:
first, arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*); second, non-arising and non-ceasing (*anutpāda-anirodha*); third, the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*); and fourth, the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

These meanings are derived from the "Chapter on Holy Conduct" (*Āryacaryā-parivarta*) of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which distinguishes these four types based on the partial and the perfect, and the phenomenal and the principle. As for what is called "arising and ceasing":

Because delusion regarding the truth is profound, [the truths] are designated according to their functional aspects; thus, although suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are one dharma, they are divided into two by way of cause and effect, and the same applies to the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states: "The resultant nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called the Truth of Suffering; their causal nature is called the Truth of Origin.

The ultimate cessation of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas is called the Truth of Cessation; all untainted (*anāsrava*) formations are called the Truth of the Path. Thus it is said in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.

The clouds and shadows of the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas) being a heavy burden, oppressive and binding, constitute the Noble Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The afflictions of craving and attachment that can summon future results constitute the Noble Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Precepts, concentration, and wisdom, as well as impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, which can eliminate the root of suffering, constitute the Noble Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

The severance of the bonds of cause and effect within the twenty-five states of existence constitutes the Noble Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). All of these clarify the characteristics of the four noble truths of arising and ceasing. Thus it is said by the Sage.

Regarding the term "Right Noble Truths" (*samyak-ārya-satya*), used to refute false teachings, there are three interpretations: first, they are called "truths" (*satya*) because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not false;
second, they are called "truths" because by seeing these four, one attains non-erroneous awakening; and third, they are called "truths" because one can manifest this Dharma to others.
As the *Mahā-sūtra* states: "Ordinary worldlings possess suffering but lack the truths; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas [possess both suffering and the truths]..."

To perceive suffering as suffering and the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) is to know that ordinary beings do not see the noble principle; they do not attain wisdom and cannot speak [of it], perceiving only suffering without the reality of "Truth.

Because the Śrāvakas possess these three meanings, it is called "Truth" (satya). As for non-arising (anutpāda): because their delusion regarding the True is slight, it is named according to the Principle.

Suffering has no characteristic of oppression; Accumulation (samudaya) has no characteristic of conjunction; the Path (mārga) has no characteristic of duality; and Cessation (nirodha) [has no characteristic of extinction].

Furthermore, one should practice and correspond with the mark of non-arising (*anutpāda-lakṣaṇa*) regarding suffering and emptiness; the three are likewise so. Moreover, as for "non-arising," "arising" is a name for the origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*).
Since the origin and the path are themselves emptiness, they do not arise. When the origin and the path do not arise, there is no suffering.

Extinction (*nirodha*) is the reality (*tattva*) within the phenomenon itself, not a reality that exists after extinction. As the Great Sūtra says: "The various Bodhisattvas understand that suffering is without suffering; therefore, it does not exist."
Suffering possesses the true reality; the other three [truths] are likewise so. Therefore, they are called the Four Noble Truths of Non-arising. Regarding "immeasurable":
because it is heavy within delusion, it receives its name from its activity. Suffering has immeasurable aspects, for the fruits of the ten dharma-realms are not the same.
Accumulation has immeasurable aspects, for the afflictions of the five abodes are not the same. The Path has immeasurable aspects, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
Because the Buddha-dharma is not uniform, the cessation [of suffering] possesses immeasurable characteristics; because the various *pāramitās* are not uniform, the *Mahā-sūtra* states:

"To know that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are suffering is called middle wisdom; to discern that the aggregates possess immeasurable characteristics is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
I have not at all expounded this in that sūtra. The third [case] is likewise thus; this is called the immeasurable.
The Four Noble Truths have no creator; because they are subtle within delusion, they are named according to principle.
Since one is deluded regarding this principle, awakening is called the truth of affliction (*kleśa-satya*), and nirvana is called the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Because one can understand [this], afflictions are themselves awakening, termed the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), and birth-and-death are themselves nirvana, termed the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Thus, while abiding in phenomena, there is no conceptualization.

Because it is without thought and without anyone who creates it, it is called "uncreated. A great sutra states: "The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one speaks of two truths in accordance with sentient beings; those who have left the world know that this is the ultimate truth.
As for the "one true truth," it is without falsehood and without inversion, characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, it is so named.
These constitute the four noble truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Second, regarding the judgment of the coarse and the subtle: the treatises of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not present truths beyond these four. If the teaching, practice, and realization are not integrated, it is coarse;
even if the teaching is integrated but practice and realization are not, it is still coarse. Only when all three are integrated is it subtle. This may be understood by reference to the five flavors.
[This is] known.
Regarding the three modes of manifestation, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The arising of arising is ineffable, up to the non-arising of non-arising is ineffable;
yet because there are causes and conditions, it can also be spoken of. Alternatively, three types may be spoken of as coarse, while one may be spoken of as [subtle]."
The three subtle [elements] cannot be said to be coarse, nor can the one coarse [element] be said to be subtle;

or all four may be said to be coarse, or all four may be said to be subtle; or all four may be said to have both coarse and subtle aspects, or all four may be said not to have both coarse and subtle aspects;
or all four may be said to be neither coarse nor subtle, or all four may be said not to be neither coarse nor subtle.
The coarse is not the subtle; through such various [distinctions], all are definitively resolved into the entry into the subtle, wherein the provisional is opened and the real is revealed.

That all four are "inexpressible" refers to the loftiness of their stage; that all four are "expressible" refers to the vastness of their essence; that all four are both "expressible" and "inexpressible" refers to the length of their function;
and that all four are neither expressible nor inexpressible refers to that which is neither lofty, nor vast, nor long, nor short.
It is neither one nor different; it is collectively termed "wondrous. This can be understood by contemplating the mind.
Regarding the four points concerning the Two Truths as the Fourfold Unity: first, a brief explanation of the three meanings; second, the formal explanation of the Two Truths;

third, the judgment of the coarse and the wondrous; and fourth, the opening of the coarse to reveal the wondrous. First, the brief explanation of the three meanings refers to: following sentiment, following sentiment-and-wisdom, and following wisdom; these correspond to following sentiment, following wisdom, and following both.
The dispositions of those who speak differ, and their speech varies according to those dispositions; it is like showing various things to a blind person to indicate "milk.

Upon hearing these differing accounts, the blind person disputes over the color white—how could that color itself be milk? For one whose wisdom follows such dispositions, they claim there are two truths, both of which are conventional.
Only when one awakens to the principle of truth can it be called ultimate (*paramārtha*); the ultimate is simply the One. It is like the five hundred bhikṣus, each [perceiving differently].
Regarding the explanation of the causes of the body, the causes of the body are manifold; however, the correct principle is singular. A sutra states:

"That which is perceived by the minds of worldly people is called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); that which is perceived by the minds of those who have transcended the world is called ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Such an explanation refers to the two truths according to sentiment and wisdom.
As for those who follow wisdom, the sages who realize the principle not only perceive the true [ultimate], but are also able to comprehend the conventional [relative]. As it is said:
When the eye is cleared of cataracts, one sees forms and sees emptiness; as the outflow-free wisdom becomes ever more profound, mundane knowledge is increasingly purified. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Ordinary people walk through the world without knowing the characteristics of the world, whereas the Tathāgata walks through the world clearly understanding the characteristics of the world.
This refers to the two truths according to wisdom.

Second, to correctly clarify the two truths: taking the essential meaning while omitting detail, it is sufficient for the purpose to point to *dharmatā* as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and ignorance and the twelve links of dependent origination as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
However, because the human mind is coarse and shallow and fails to perceive its profound subtlety, one must further expand upon this by discussing seven types of the two truths.
The first is: that which exists substantially is conventional; the cessation of substantial existence is [ultimate].

1. The two truths are: that which is illusory existence is the conventional, and that which is the emptiness of illusory existence is the ultimate. 2. The two truths are: that which is illusory existence is the conventional, and that which is the emptiness of illusory existence—where emptiness and non-emptiness are co-present—is the ultimate. 3. The two truths are:

that which is illusory existence is the conventional, and that which is the emptiness of illusory existence where all phenomena tend toward both emptiness and non-emptiness is the ultimate. 4. The two truths are: that which is illusory existence and that which is the emptiness of illusory existence are both called the conventional;

[the realization that] all phenomena tend toward both emptiness and non-emptiness is the ultimate. 5. That which is illusory existence and that which is the emptiness of illusory existence are both named... [the conventional].
6. That the conventional is neither existent nor empty is the True; that the illusory existence of the conventional is itself emptiness—all such are termed conventional.
That all phenomena tend toward being neither existent nor empty is the True. 7. That the illusory existence of the conventional is itself emptiness—all such are conventional.
That all phenomena tend toward existence, tend toward emptiness, and tend toward being neither existent nor empty is Real Existence.

Regarding the two truths: the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all real dharmas; because they constitute the myriad phenomena that pervade the universe, they are termed the "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).

Once this conventionality has been extinguished through the path of skillful cultivation, one then attains union with the Real. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Emptiness is form, and form is emptiness.

Because conventional reality is extinguished, it is called "emptiness as form"; because form is not extinguished, it is called "form as emptiness. This is the teaching for those within the midst of illness.
The fact that within the letters of the "medicine-less" there is no bodhi is precisely this meaning; it constitutes the characteristic of the two truths as ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).

Based on this, one may also understand it by inferring through the three meanings of "following sentiment," "sentiment-intelligence," and "intelligence. As for the two truths of illusion and emptiness, this refutes the previous intention.
Why? Because when [the former] exists, the true [truth] is absent; when [the latter] exists, the conventional [truth] is absent. Thus, the two truths are not simultaneous.

If the meaning [of the two truths] is not established by clarifying that things are illusory existents (*māyopama*), then since illusory existence is conventional and illusory existence is unattainable, the conventional is itself the ultimate.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Because emptiness and form are mutually identical, the meaning of the two truths is established.

This is called the two truths of the emptiness of illusory existence. Regarding the two truths of the emptiness and non-emptiness of illusory existence, the conventional is no different from what preceded.
Regarding the truth, there are three distinct types; the conventional follows these three truths, thus forming the Threefold Two Truths. What are their characteristics?

As clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, that which is neither outflowing (*āsrava*) nor non-outflowing: first, "neither outflowing" means it is not the conventional; "neither non-outflowing" serves to eliminate attachment. Why is this?

Because when a practitioner conditions upon the non-outflowing, they give rise to clinging—just as one gives rise to latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) by conditioning upon cessation—and [this phrase] serves to destroy such [clinging].
The mind that clings [to these] returns to enter the outflow-free (*anāsrava*); this is one set of two truths.

Next, another person hears "neither outflowing nor outflow-free" and understands it as being distinct from the two extremes, manifesting the principle of the Middle Way; since the Middle Way is the Truth, this is another set of two truths.

Furthermore, another person hears "neither with outflows nor without outflows" and immediately knows that this double negation correctly manifests the Middle Way, which is the Dharma of the Middle Way.
The power and function of the realms are as vast as space; that all phenomena tend toward being neither outflowing (*āsrava*) nor non-outflowing is yet another aspect of the two truths.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "Śrāvakas see only emptiness and do not see non-emptiness;
the wise see both emptiness and non-emptiness. This is precisely that meaning. The Two Vehicles [erroneously] claim that one must destroy this emptiness because they are attached to it.
Because they are attached to emptiness, it is said that "emptiness is not empty. If this attachment is destroyed, one merely sees emptiness and does not see non-emptiness.

For those of sharp faculties, because non-emptiness is called "wondrous existence," it is said that "non-emptiness is not empty. When those of superior faculties hear of non-emptiness, they take it to mean the *tathāgatagarbha*, wherein all phenomena converge in the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Returning to the categories of emptiness and non-emptiness, there are thus three types [of views]. II.

Furthermore, regarding the truth (*satya*), if one distinguishes three types of differences based on the principle that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) tend toward that which is neither outflowing (*āsrava*) nor non-outflowing (*anāsrava*):

First, when a person hears that all phenomena tend toward that which is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, they think that all phenomena are no different from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and circulate throughout the ten directions of the world-system, yet remain right where they are, like a water jar.
Second, another person, upon hearing "tending toward," understands that the principle herein requires the arrival of all conditioned practices (*saṃskāra*).
When one proceeds toward [enlightenment], others hear that all destinies (*gati*) are neither outflows (*āsrava*) nor non-outflows, yet they are endowed with all phenomena.
Therefore, it is said that this single conventional truth revolves according to the three truths: whether facing a single truth, a composite truth, or the inconceivable truth;
through infinite modalities, it turns flexibly to meet the capacities of beings, appearing and disappearing to benefit them, and each instance possesses [this quality].

Regarding the three meanings of "following sentiment," "sentiment," and "wisdom": if one follows wisdom to realize the conventional, and as wisdom turns, realizes the partial truth, this constitutes the wisdom that penetrates both truths;
if one realizes the non-empty ultimate truth, this constitutes the distinct entry into the wisdom that penetrates both truths;

and if one realizes the non-empty ultimate truth of all realms of existence, this constitutes the perfect entry into the wisdom that penetrates both truths. The entry into wisdom by these three types of persons differs and is further restricted.

The illumination of the conventional is also distinct from the illusory existence of the unconditioned. To hold that the conventional is neither existent nor non-existent, while the ultimate is neither existent nor non-existent, is because both existence and non-existence constitute the conventional middle way;

whereas being neither existent nor non-existent and non-dual constitutes the ultimate. When the followers of the Two Vehicles hear of this, they fail to understand either the ultimate or the conventional;
thus they are like the mute and the deaf. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "When I and Maitreya discussed the worldly truth, five hundred [monks]..."

The Śrāvaka refers to the teaching of the True Truth (satyārtha), which is precisely this meaning. Regarding the "perfect entry into the two distinct truths": the conventional truth is the same as that of the distinct [vehicle], but the True Truth differs.
The person of the distinct [vehicle] maintains that it is merely the principle of non-emptiness (*aśūnyatā*).

To manifest this principle, one must rely on the skillful means of cultivation; therefore, it is said that "all dharmas tend toward non-emptiness. When the person of the Perfect [Vehicle] hears the principle of non-emptiness, they immediately know that it is endowed with the One.
Because all Buddha-dharmas are without deficiency or diminution, it is said that "all destinies are not empty.
Regarding the Two Truths of the Perfect Teaching, they are explained directly as the inconceivable Two Truths. The True is precisely the Conventional, and the Conventional is precisely the True.

The wish-fulfilling jewel serves as a metaphor for the True, while its function serves as a metaphor for the Conventional. Thus, the jewel is the function, and the function is the jewel; they are non-dual yet dual.
This merely distinguishes between the ultimate and the conventional.

Third, regarding the judgment of the coarse and the subtle: in reality, there are two truths. The "half-syllable" (*ardha-akṣara*) dharma-gate leads those of dull faculties to discard the dung of conceptual proliferation;
because the meaning of the two truths is not yet established therein, this dharma is considered coarse. The "full-syllable" (*pūrṇa-akṣara*) dharma-gate of the two truths [is like] an illusion.

For the sake of teaching those of sharp faculties regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, these three types of persons attain together what was previously considered subtle; they equally perceive only emptiness.

However, that which follows is coarse, because entering through the distinct [teachings] allows one to perceive non-emptiness, which is thus considered subtle. Since the discourse on principle in that [former] teaching is not fully integrated, it is therefore deemed coarse.
Entering through the perfect [teaching] is considered subtle; this subtlety does not differ from what follows, as it incorporates the provisional expedients of the distinct teachings.

The coarse [teaching] distinguishes the two truths without incorporating the provisional means; therefore, it is called the "wondrous teaching. When discussing principle, that which is not yet harmonized with the particular is coarse, while that which enters the particular and is harmonized is wondrous.
That which incorporates the provisional means of the particular is coarse, whereas the two truths of the Perfect [Teaching] alone—direct and supreme—are wondrous.

Next, regarding the judgment of the coarse and the wondrous according to the emotions and the wisdom, first concerning the Tripiṭaka: [The text continues: ...first, regarding the Tripiṭaka... (as per the provided fragment).

Because those who hear [the teachings] cling to the two truths according to their own conceptions, taking words that express reality to be false speech, they give rise to views regarding speech; thus, birth and death are vast and boundless, and there is no trace of the Dharma within them.

If one can diligently cultivate the foundations of mindfulness and develop the four roots of goodness, then at that time, the two truths according to conception are both called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).

Once the untainted [wisdom] is produced, the two truths illuminated by it are all called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*). This is from the perspective of those who have attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka].

That which is illuminated by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*)—both the ultimate and the conventional—is termed the "Two Truths according to Wisdom" (*jñānānuvartin-satya-dvaya*). According to worldly sentiment, they are coarse; according to wisdom, they are subtle.
This is like churning milk to first produce curd: once the curd is formed, the mind and its objects accord with one another, and entering and emerging [from meditative states] becomes effortless.

Thus, one attains the "equality of sentiment and wisdom" (*citta-jñāna-samatā*), whereby the provisional teachings are explained through the common and the particular, and entry into the common leads to the perfect. Entering the common causes them to...

Shameful of their smallness and aspiring toward greatness, they lamented their own status as "ruined seeds" and thirstily yearned for the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*). At that time, it was as if curd were being transformed into fresh butter; their minds gradually became open and at ease.

Thereupon, according to their dispositions, their emotions, and their wisdom—whether equal or otherwise—he taught the Distinct and Perfect [teachings]. Entering the Distinct, he clarified the uncommon *prajñā*.

Having been commanded to take charge of the family estate, he was made to understand all matters of gold, silver, and precious treasures, including their acquisition, expenditure, and management. Once he understood these things, [he attained realization].
This is like the transformation of fresh butter (*navanīta*) into matured butter (*ghṛta*); after a long time, the Buddhas must necessarily teach the ultimate truth (*tattva*).

Thus, they teach the two truths—both conventional and ultimate—in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings and the levels of their cognition and wisdom. This is like the transformation of matured butter into clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Although these six types of two-truth teachings ripen sentient beings and result in four flavors, they are therefore considered coarse compared to the single flavor of clarified butter.

This is indeed subtle. Furthermore, regarding the provisional judgment of the coarse and the subtle: although the first two teachings contain elements that accord with wisdom (*jñāna*), they are exclusively teachings that accord with worldly sentiment (*saṃvṛti*) and are spoken with the intention of conveying another's meaning;

Regarding the six kinds of ghee, five are coarse and one is subtle; the *Lotus Sūtra* contains only the One Vehicle and the Two Truths, lacking the six provisional means and possessing only the subtle without the coarse—it is for this reason that its title is called "Subtle.
This constitutes the judgment of the coarse and the subtle based on mutual relativity (*āpekṣika*).

Fourth, regarding "manifestation": the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time originally appeared in the world for the great causal purpose of enabling sentient beings to manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that the meaning of the lotus flower emerging from the water is inexhaustible:
because it emerges from the muddy waters of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), it enters into the great assembly of the Tathāgata and sits among them, just as the various bodhisattvas sit.
Those who hear the teaching of supreme, pure wisdom upon the lotus are certainly not sitting on its petals;

rather, it is the various bodhisattvas who, having heard the teaching of the single perfect path and realized the single perfect fruit within the realm of the Lotus King, sit together with Śākyamuni Buddha upon the lotus pedestal.
Such is the Buddha’s intention. Only when they first see my body and first hear the One Reality do they enter the flower.
For those who have not yet entered, the platform is opened from the outset through gradual stages;

furthermore, by employing various other skillful means (*upāya*) to assist in manifesting the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*), he preaches the two truths—whether single or combined, or inconceivable and diverse in their differences—all of which serve as skillful means for the Lotus Platform.
This does not merely begin at the Deer Park, nor does it stop at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); it has been so from the very beginning.
From the time the Buddha first came into this world until his original practice of the bodhisattva path, he has employed the expedient means of the "flower pedestal" for the sake of sentient beings.
The text states: "In the past, I established a vow that all sentient beings without exception should likewise attain this Way.

One should know that these introductory verses are not merely for the present; those who were originally transformed and led into the flower pedestal constitute one aspect [of his work], while those who have not yet... [are another].
As for those who enter, it is as described above regarding the uninterrupted skillful means; the intermediate stages are likewise so.

Whether one enters from the *Avataṃsaka*, the Vaipulya, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, or other sutras—whether entering through the Separate (Biaobie), the Common (Tong), or the Perfect (Yuan) vehicles, or entering the Separate and the Perfect, or entering the Lotus Platform (*Huatai*)—this is no different from the original entry.
Furthermore, this constitutes one side [of the path]. As for those who have not yet entered, they are all brought to maturity through the four flavors (*sīwei*) within this very context.

Among the various teachings that lead one to enter the Lotus Terrace (*padmavimāna*), whether one abides in three flavors, two flavors, or a single flavor, or is born there in its entirety, all coarse elements are resolved into the sublime so that they all enter the Lotus Terrace.
While it is difficult to break what has been preserved by the Tripiṭaka and difficult to open what has already been broken, how much more so for that which is easy to break and easy to open?
All things follow their conditions while remaining as they are; when the reality (*tattva*) is revealed through the specific gateway appropriate to each, one immediately enters the Lotus Terrace.

The text states: "Seven-jeweled great chariots, immeasurable in number, were each bestowed upon the sons. This refers to the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real (*kai-gen*), wherein all that is coarse is made sublime;
it is the "sublime beyond dependence" (*zettai-myō*).
Fifth, the elucidation of the three truths as three: first, the elucidation of the three truths; second, the judgment of the three; third, the opening of the two previous types of two-truths.
Because the Middle Way is not clearly understood, one may approach it through the fivefold Two Truths; thus, there are five types of Three Truths.
By distinguishing between the particular and the universal, the meaning of the Three Truths—neither outflowing (*sāsrava*) nor non-outflowing (*anāsrava*)—is established:

that which is outflowing is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), that which is non-outflowing is the ultimate (*paramārtha*), and that which is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing is the Middle. According to the discourse of this specific teaching, it merely differs from emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Regarding the "Middle" [Truth] that is effortless (*anābhoga*) yet does not fully encompass all phenomena and enters the three truths universally: it is not different from the previous "Two Truths.
It is neither outflowing (*āsava*) nor non-outflowing, and it possesses all phenomena; this differs from the previous "Middle. Regarding the "Middle" that separately enters the three truths:

it opens up that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) into two truths and, in contrast to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), establishes the Middle as the principle itself. Regarding the "Middle" that universally enters the separate three truths: it is the Two [Truths].
The truths are no different from the aforementioned point that the Middle Truth is fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma; the three truths are perfect in this way.

Not only is the Middle Truth fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma, but the True and the Conventional are likewise so. The three truths are perfectly interfused such that one is three and three are one, as explained in the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation).

Second, regarding the judgment of coarse and subtle: the Separate and Perfect [teachings] are coarse because they enter through the Shared and carry its expedient means; the Separate [teaching] is subtle when it does not carry the Shared;

the Perfect [teaching] is coarse when it enters through the Separate and carries its expedient means; and the Perfect [teaching] is most subtle when it does not carry expedient means. Regarding the five-flavored teachings:
the Milk Teaching speaks of three kinds of Threefold Truths—two are coarse and one is subtle; the Curd Teaching is entirely coarse; both Butters are... [subtle].
The five kinds of the three truths consist of four "coarse" and one "sublime. This sutra possesses only one kind: the sublime truth of mutual dependence (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Regarding the threefold revelation and manifestation: it definitively resolves the aforementioned various coarse levels into the sublime three truths; as there is nothing further to which they can be relative, this constitutes the truth of absolute transcendence (*atyantāpekṣā*).
Excellent.

Sixth, regarding the clarification of the Single Truth (*ekasatya*): The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "What is called the Two Truths is in fact one; it is spoken of as two as a skillful means (*upāya*).

It is like a person who, while still intoxicated and before the dizziness has subsided, sees the sun and moon revolving, and thus claims there is both a revolving sun and a non-revolving sun. One who is sober sees only [the single truth]."
The non-turning does not perceive turning; these two—turning and non-turning—are coarse, while non-turning is subtle. The Three Piṭakas are entirely turning;
the various Mahāyāna sūtras contain both turning and non-turning, with one part being non-turning.
This present sūtra, however, directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the Unsurpassed Way, which is exclusively non-turning and thus truly subtle. All truths are ultimately inexpressible.
Since all dharmas have from the very beginning been characterized by constant, inherent quiescence, how could there be the various truths with their manifold characteristics and mutual obstructions?
If even a single truth does not exist, how could there be multiple truths? Each and every one is ineffable. To say it is expressible is coarse;
to say it is inexpressible is subtle. Even "inexpressible" is inexpressible. That this is subtle is itself subtle, for the path of language has been cut off.

If one speaks generally of that which is "inexpressible," then from "birth-and-birth" being inexpressible up to "neither-birth-nor-non-birth" being inexpressible, the preceding inexpressibles are considered coarse, while "neither-birth-nor-non-birth" being inexpressible is considered subtle.

If the coarse and the subtle were distinct and merely relative without merging, they would not be non-dual; rather, their non-duality constitutes the "sublime beyond dependence. Regarding the five flavors, this refers to the first, the Milk Teaching.

The coarse ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is one; the subtle ultimate truth is the *dadhi* (curd) teaching, which is one; the coarse ultimate truth is the *maṇḍa* (cream) [teaching], which is three;

the coarse ultimate truth is one and the subtle ultimate truth is the *ghṛta* (butter) [teaching], which is two; the coarse ultimate truth is one and the subtle ultimate truth is this sutra, which is only one subtle ultimate truth that opens up the coarse as previously asked.
Why are the Great and Small Vehicles discussed together regarding the ultimate truth? The *Śāstra* explains: "It does not subvert the noble [truths]."

Those who have attained *nirvāṇa* within their own minds yet cling to it as something not yet attained give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding *nirvāṇa*, like the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take non-arising as their object;
therefore, [the text] refutes them by stating that there is no truth. Question: If that is so, then both attainment and non-attainment in the Hīnayāna are equally refuted;
should attainment and non-attainment in the Mahāyāna likewise be refuted? Answer: They are not comparable, for the Hīnayāna still possesses distinct afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because it can be eliminated and its distinct principle can be revealed, although one has attained [the Middle Way], one must still refute [extreme views]. If this were not so, how could one refute them? Question:
If that is the case, the Middle Way should consist of only one true reality (*satya*); one should not say that there is no truth. Answer:

For those who have not yet attained [it], they harbor delusions within their attachments; therefore, "no-truth" (*asatya*) is required. For those who have truly attained it, there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Second, regarding the excellence of wisdom (*jñāna-viśeṣa*): the ultimate principle is profound and subtle; it cannot be manifested without wisdom, yet wisdom can know that which is not within the realm [of ordinary cognition].

When the realm is integrated, the wondrous wisdom is likewise designated as such. Therefore, following the discussion of the realm, wisdom is explained in six aspects: first, number; second, category; third, characteristic; fourth, illumination;
fifth, discernment; and sixth, opening.
The enumerations are: first, the wisdom of worldly knowledge; second, the wisdom of the five stages of stabilizing the mind and the four foundations of mindfulness;

third, the wisdom of the four roots of goodness; fourth, the wisdom of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path; fifth, the wisdom of the pratyekabuddha; sixth, the wisdom of the six pāramitās; seventh, the wisdom of the śrāvaka who realizes the nature of phenomena through the skillful means of entering the truth; eighth, the wisdom of the pratyekabuddha who realizes the nature of phenomena;

ninth, the wisdom of the bodhisattva who realizes the nature of phenomena and enters the true skillful means; tenth, the wisdom of the bodhisattva who realizes the nature of phenomena and emerges into the provisional realm.

11. The wisdom of the ten levels of faith in the Separate Teaching; 12. The wisdom of the ten stages of mind in the Shared Teaching; 13. The wisdom of the ten bhūmis; 14. The wisdom of the Buddha in the Tripiṭaka Teaching;
15. The wisdom of the Buddha in the Shared Teaching; 16. The wisdom of the Buddha in the Separate Teaching; 17.
The wisdom of the five ranks of disciples in the Perfect Teaching; 18. The wisdom of the purification of the six sense organs; 19. The wisdom from the first stage up to Equal Enlightenment.
The twenty types of wondrous enlightened wisdom (*miao-jue-zhi*).

As for their categories: mundane wisdom (*shi-zhi*) constitutes one type because it lacks the Path, consists of false imaginings and deluded attachments, operates outside of principle, and is neither faith nor entry [into the Path].

The five stages of stabilizing the mind (*wu-ting-xin*) and the four foundations of mindfulness (*si-nian-chu*) have already entered the first stage of the Nobles (*xian*); they share the same affinity with the Buddha-dharma and are thus both considered external ordinary beings (*wai-fan*).

The four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) are treated as one because they are equally mundane noble ones (*pṛthagjana-ārya*); the four fruits (*catur-phala*) are treated as one because they equally perceive the truth (*satya-darśana*);

the single branch of the Buddha is distinguished because its contemplation of specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vipaśyanā*) can penetrate the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); the six perfections (*ṣat-pāramitā*) are treated as one because the wisdom that takes principle as its object is weak while the wisdom that takes phenomena as its object is strong;

the Śrāvakas of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) are treated as one because their wisdom of realizing the nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva-jñāna*) is superior; and the Pratyekabuddhas are further slightly superior.
Therefore, one is for the sake of the common teaching (tongjiao) Bodhisattva entering the true [reality], as they universally study the wisdom of the four gates;
one is for the sake of the common teaching Bodhisattva emerging into the conventional (chujia), as their wisdom correctly takes the mundane as its object;

one is for the sake of the distinct teaching (biejiao) stage of the ten faiths (shixin), as their wisdom first knows the Middle Way, being superior before and inferior after; and one is for the sake of the thirty minds of the distinct teaching, as all are internal ordinary beings (neifan). Thus, there are ten.

Because the ground is identical as the noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), it constitutes one [aspect]; because the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka is in the position of a teacher while the followers of the Three Vehicles are disciples, it constitutes one;

because the wisdom of the Shared Teaching Buddha excels in severing delusions and illuminating capacities, it constitutes one; because the wisdom of the Distinct Teaching Buddha is further superior, it constitutes one;
and because the five grades of disciples of the Perfect Teaching all possess afflictions yet are able to know the secret of the Tathāgata, it constitutes one.
Because it is the treasury [of all wisdoms], it constitutes one; because it is the pure wisdom of the six sense organs that borders upon the Truth, it constitutes one;

because from the first stage up to Equal Enlightenment they collectively break through ignorance, it constitutes one; and because the Buddha-wisdom of Wondrous Enlightenment is unsurpassed and most honored, it constitutes one.
Third, regarding the discernment of characteristics: the worldly wisdom of India reaches its ultimate limit in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

What our own tradition venerates as essential consists of loyalty and filial piety, the five constant virtues (*pañca-guṇa*), the six arts (*ṣaḍ-vidyā-sthāna*), astronomy, geography, medicine, divination, military strategy, commerce, and the knowledge of a thousand species of plants;

they recognize the names of ten thousand varieties of birds and beasts. Furthermore, whether they smear their left side or cut their right, they are free from hatred or attachment, having attained the fundamental [wisdom].

The concentration that gives rise to the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) includes: stopping the flow of the Ganges with one’s ear; transforming Śakra into a sheep; swallowing wind and clouds; and reaching out to touch the sun and moon.

Such dharmas belong to worldly concentration (laukika-samādhi). Because this concentration is unmoving and its wisdom is unmoving, yet it seeks fame and profit and increases views and craving, it is known by the name "worldly knowledge" (loka-jñāna).
Regarding the five cessations (pañca-sthāpanā) and the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni), they are so called because they possess concentration.

Because one possesses wisdom while remaining still, it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). Contemplation can overturn false views, concentration can restrain distraction, counting the breath treats scattering, the foul (*aśubha*) treats greed, loving-kindness and compassion treat anger, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) treats ignorance, and mindfulness of the Buddha treats obstacles to the Path. The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) constitute contemplation;
the four superior knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding the Truth of Suffering treat the four inversions (*viparyāsa*). Since the four inversions do not arise, these four contemplations first overturn them.

Because one has not yet entered the principle of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is called the "knowledge of the external ordinary person" (*bāhyapṛthagjana-jñāna*). The stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) gives rise to knowledge that takes the objects of the Four Noble Truths as its domain and subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*);
like fire with smoke, it takes this initial state as its characteristic. The fire of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) likewise takes the stage of Heat as its precursor.

As for the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are like the summit of a mountain, and thus they are named "Summits. If one can draw near to the wholesome...
A friend hears from him the Dharma of the compliant skillful means and correctly contemplates it within his own mind;

he believes in the Buddha’s bodhi, believes in the well-spoken Dharma, and believes in the pure merits of the Sangha—this is called believing in the Jewels. He speaks of the impermanence of form, up to the impermanence of consciousness—this is called believing in the aggregates.
He knows that there is suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—this is called believing in the Truths. If one acts in this way, one abides [in the Dharma].

If the summit (*mūrdhan*) is not thus, it immediately regresses; therefore, one who contemplates the Dharma through patience (*kṣānti*) correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, the suffering of the form and formless realms;

the origin of formations in the desire realm, the origin of formations in the form and formless realms; the cessation of formations in the desire realm, the cessation of formations in the form and formless realms;

and the path leading to the cessation of formations in the desire realm, the path leading to the cessation of formations in the form and formless realms. In this manner, there are thirty-two moments of mind.

This is called the practice of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), wherein the practitioner subsequently diminishes their practice and objects of focus until they correctly contemplate the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) with constant continuity, without interruption or separation.
While contemplating in this manner, a profound sense of revulsion arises, and they further reduce [their focus] until they maintain only two moments of mind while contemplating a single aspect;
this is called "middle patience" (*madhya-kṣānti*). Furthermore, by means of a single moment of mind, they contemplate the suffering of the desire realm.

This is called the highest patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). Furthermore, after this, the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) arises. Following the Supreme Worldly Dharma, the "Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises next.

Regarding the first fruit, there are eight patiences and eight knowledges; regarding the [next] three fruits, there are nine uninterrupted knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*) and nine liberating knowledges (*vimukti-jñāna*) that take the truth as their object through repeated contemplation.

For the Pratyekabuddha, these function by means of both general and specific characteristics, clearly discerning suffering and its origin across the three periods of time according to the twelve links of dependent origination.

This refers to the wisdom of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The wisdom of the principle that takes the six perfections as its object is weak; it subdues but does not sever [afflictions]. The wisdom of phenomena that takes objects as its basis is strong;

it is able to relinquish body, life, and wealth without any lingering attachment. In the Śrāvaka vehicle of the Shared Teaching, one attains the truth through the single gate of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) by realizing that the conventional is identical to the ultimate.

The Pratyekabuddha is able to realize the truth by means of the single gate of both general and specific characteristics, understanding that the conventional is identical to the ultimate. The Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching is able to do so through all four gates.

Through the general and specific characteristics, one penetrates the conventional to realize the ultimate; furthermore, one universally emerges from the four gates into the provisional to teach and transform sentient beings.

Specifically, within the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), one takes the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the fruit as the object of faith. To seek this principle, one gives rise to the ten minds of faith. In the ten abidings (*vihāra*), one primarily practices emptiness while incidentally practicing the provisional and the middle.
In the ten practices (*caryā*), one primarily practices the provisional while incidentally practicing the middle. In the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), one primarily practices... [the middle].

In the middle [category], those who have realized the first stage and above undergo repeated deliberation; among them, the Tripiṭaka Buddhas exhaust both the primary afflictions and their residual habits (*vāsanā*) in a single moment by means of thirty-four moments of mind.

The Universal Buddhas (*Samyaksaṃbuddha*), while seated at the site of enlightenment, exhaust the remaining residual habit-energies through the wisdom of "one-moment correspondence" (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*).
The Particular Buddhas (*Pratyekabuddha*) exhaust the final grade of ignorance through the "subsequent diamond-like mind" (*vajropama-citta*) and thereby achieve ultimate Buddhahood and perfection.

Those in the five stages possess afflictions yet are able to know the Tathāgata’s secret treasury; those at the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties attain a semblance of the wisdom of the Middle Way;
those in the first stage attain the Tathāgata’s single body as infinite bodies and enter the ocean-like flow of the Dharma, wherein their practice flows spontaneously;
subsequent stages are easily understood.

Regarding the fourth point, the illumination of objects by wisdom: if one holds that objects are illuminated by wisdom, or that wisdom is produced by objects, all four permutations fall into the trap of substantialism (*svabhāva*).

If objects and wisdom are established through the causes and conditions of the four *siddhāntas*, they exist merely as names; thus, wisdom can illuminate objects, and objects likewise illuminate wisdom.
As the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states: "That which is called wisdom and the locus of wisdom are both termed *prajñā*. Let us set aside this matter for now.

The wisdom that illuminates the ten suchnesses of the six realms through the five *sthāpanā* concentrations is the wisdom of the "going to the essence of phenomena" (*dharmatā-gamana*); this constitutes seven types of wisdom.

The wisdom that illuminates the ten suchnesses of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) through the six *pāramitās* and the bodhisattvas who emerge from the provisional teaching (*sāmānyayāna*) belongs to both categories, as it involves the upward-seeking illumination of the bodhisattva’s ten suchnesses and the downward-transforming illumination of the ten suchnesses of the six realms.

The forty mental states (*citta-kṣaṇa*) of the distinct teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*) also belong to both categories, as they involve the illumination of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as described above.
The two types of wisdom belong to sequential illumination, which illuminates the ten suchnesses of bodhisattvas; non-sequential illumination illuminates the ten suchnesses of Buddhas.

Regarding the five stages that transcend the ordinary, all four wisdoms illuminate the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm. In summary, these twenty wisdoms illuminate the four kinds of twelvefold dependent origination:
namely, mundane wisdom, the five stopping-meditations, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], up to the pratyekabuddha, and the six perfections.
The Buddha of the Tripiṭaka possesses seven wisdoms that illumine the realm of the conditioned arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination;

this is the expedient wisdom for entering the truth and the wisdom for emerging into the provisional [provisional] common teaching for the three vehicles. The Buddha possesses five wisdoms that illumine the realm of the conditioned dependent origination that is neither born nor extinguished.
The Buddha of the Distinct Teaching possesses four wisdoms that illumine the inconceivable arising... [of the ten stages of faith, the thirty minds, and the ten grounds].
