Because the ten realms necessarily interact with one another and relate to both self and other, and because they correspond to the aforementioned ten realms in terms of self and other,
it is known that the principle of the mind’s contemplation and its responsive resonance is complete.

Regarding the seventh point, the "wondrousness of supernatural powers," the previous treatise on the capacity for response merely distinguished the characteristics of what can be generated and what can be reached.

If one correctly discusses the transformative function of benefiting others, it refers to the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels: the wheel of body, the wheel of speech, and the wheel of the other's mind.
Although the "Universal Gate" chapter contains only two textual passages, they simultaneously encompass these three meanings. To roam within the Sahā world is the wheel of body;
to preach the Dharma is the wheel of speech; and to see the lotus flowers is to know that the depth of the great pond is profound—this is the wheel of the other's mind.
If one sees that the teaching of the Dharma is great, one knows that wisdom is likewise great; thus, both wheels are shown together, which is the wheel of the other's mind.
To show the wheel of the body is to manifest the body of the King of Medicine Trees and the King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels.
To show the wheel of speech is to manifest the Poison Drum and the Celestial Drum. This is because compassion permeates the body and speech, whereby two bodies are manifested.

The two drums proclaim and spread [the teaching] as if manifesting the mind-wheel; this is also equivalent to the "acting according to one's own intent" and the "acting according to the intent of others," which likewise correspond to the "sick-child-like conduct.
Above, the mutual resonance between the capacity and the response has been distinguished, yet the subtle principle remains difficult to reveal;

it must therefore be activated by spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) to manifest auspicious signs that secretly symbolize the principle. Regarding what is termed "spiritual power," the *Yingluo jing* states: "Spirit..."
"Mind" (*citta*) refers to the meaning of being difficult to fathom and know; "pervasion" (*abhijñā*) refers to the meaning of being unobstructed.
The *Dharaṇī-śvara-rāja-sūtra* states that "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi*) means it is difficult to fathom and know, while "pervasion" means there is no obstruction.

As for the differences: beings in the realm of ghosts obtain spiritual powers as a karmic retribution, whereas humans can also obtain them by taking medicine. Furthermore, external paths also possess such powers.
The Path relies upon the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) to also produce the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The various heavens possess supernormal powers obtained as retribution (*vipākaja*).

The Two Vehicles rely upon the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) to cultivate the fourteen transformations and thereby produce the supernormal powers. Bodhisattvas of the six perfections obtain five supernormal powers through dhyāna;

at the time they sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they are able to obtain the six supernormal powers. Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching obtain five supernormal powers through dhyāna by relying on the essence (*tattva*).

The Dharma-wisdom (Dharmamati) attains the untainted supernormal powers (*anāsrava-abhijñā*). In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra*), prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), one relies on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to develop the five supernormal powers;

upon entering the stages, one truly develops the untainted supernormal powers, which spontaneously and constantly illuminate all Buddha-lands without perceiving them through dualistic characteristics.

Regarding the supernormal powers in the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-vyavahāra*), according to this sutra and the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra* (Puxian guan), the faculties of the nose and tongue are included to complete the number six; thus, the knowledge of others' minds and the recollection of past lives are subsumed within the mental faculty (*manas*).
The universal penetration encompassed by the faculties does not arise based on mundane dhyāna; rather, this is the true reality of the Middle Way.

Because it is spontaneously accomplished through its own inherent penetration, it is called "unconditioned transformative dhyāna" (*avyākṛta-nirmāṇa-nirmāṇa-dhyāna*). Since it does not involve deliberate mental application, it is termed "unconditioned.

It is spontaneously and constantly luminous, like the musical instruments of the asuras that manifest further transformations from their own manifestations; thus it is called "transformative-transformation," the true reality of the Middle Way.

The supernatural power (*abhijñā*) of spontaneous engagement is distinct from other powers; its cultivation consists entirely in taking as its object the principle of the eternally abiding true reality (*dharmatā*).

As the text states: "One attains this constant eye-faculty, which is pure. The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* says: "That is to say, the eye-faculty is at all times fully possessed and never diminished by the Tathāgatas;
through its cultivation, one sees with perfect clarity and distinction," and so on, up to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
All [beings] constantly and fully possess, without deficiency, the practice of clear and distinct hearing and knowing that is equal to that [of the Buddhas].
To the Buddha, they are himself; to sentient beings, they are "others. That which sentient beings regard as impermanent is, for the Tathāgata, permanent.
Cultivation based on dhyāna is called "deficient cultivation"; cultivation based on the true mark (dharmatā) is called "non-deficient cultivation," wherein one does not perceive a Buddha.
The nature (*prakṛti*) is called "not clearly seeing"; if one sees the Buddha-nature, it is called "clearly seeing.

Furthermore, seeing the principle of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is called "clearly cognizing," while seeing the phenomena of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is called "distinctly seeing. There are two kinds of seeing: first, semblance-seeing, as explained in the section on the purification of the six sense organs;
second, true seeing, as elucidated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, referring to the Buddha’s eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

In this sutra, it is also clarified that the true body possesses the power of supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*). This refers to the "universal manifestation of the form-body" (*rūpakāya*), which manifests as a body pleasing to all sentient beings;
this is the external-body penetration. Furthermore, manifesting the body such that the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear within it—like within lapis lazuli—is the internal-body penetration.
Other instances of the manifestation of the various sense organs, both internally and externally, may be understood by analogy.
This constitutes the distinction of the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which differs from what was previously explained.

In using supernatural powers to deliver sentient beings, one does not merely transform one's own body to accord with their primary retribution (*zhengbao*); one also transforms one's own land to accord with their secondary retribution (*yi bao*). As the *Yingluo jing* states:
"Arising all lands to respond to all sentient beings. This "responding" that accords with the primary retribution refers precisely to manifesting the ten dharmas.
If the realms and forms should correspond to the shared environment (*sādhāraṇa-niśraya*), this means they are identical to the locus upon which the ten dharma-realms depend.
If they should correspond to the bodies of the four evil destinies, one employs the contemplation of evil karma and the permeation of compassion to transform the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind;

through the meditative concentration of transformation, one should manifest the forms of hell-beings and so forth, even up to the images of asuras, such that each individual sees them and perceives their activities as being identical to one's own. If they should correspond to humans...

Regarding the celestial body (*devakāya*): by means of contemplating good karma and being permeated by compassion, one employs the transformative meditative concentration (*nirmāṇa-dhyāna*) of the indeterminate to produce a body for the path of goodness, such that each person perceives it according to their own activities.
If it is appropriate to manifest as a member of the Tripiṭaka or the Two Vehicles, one uses the meditative concentration of analytical emptiness (*vibhajya-śūnyatā*) permeated by compassion;

through the indeterminate transformative meditative concentration, one arises in the form of an aged bhikṣu to participate in the *poṣadha* ceremony with the Saṃgha, and so forth. If it is appropriate to be universal...
For those of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha), one employs the compassion that is identical with the provisional and identical with the middle to permeate them.

For those of the Perfect Teaching (Bodhisattva), one employs the compassion that is identical with the middle to permeate them. Regarding the meditative concentration of the unconditioned transformation and further transformations, each perceives it as being identical to their own activity;
they know this to be identical to their primary retribution, which is beyond description or record, yet can be known by the mind and cannot be expressed in words.
If you grasp this meaning and look toward the teachings on the five flavors, the supernatural powers employed in the *Kṣīra* (Milk) teaching—whether many or few—merely express two meanings:
one coarse and one subtle. In the *Tripiṭaka*, the supernatural powers used—whether many or few—are solely for the sake of the single coarse [meaning].
In the *Vaipulya*, there are three coarse and one subtle; in the *Prajñā*, there are two coarse and one subtle. This sutra, however, is intended solely for the one subtle [meaning].
Therefore, in the "Introductory Chapter," there are ten auspicious signs, all of which symbolize the following: the entire ground being adorned and pure symbolizes the excellence of the principle;

the emission of light from between the eyebrows symbolizes the excellence of wisdom; the entry into samādhi symbolizes the excellence of practice; the heavens raining four kinds of flowers symbolizes the excellence of the stages;

the sandalwood-scented wind symbolizes the excellence of the vehicle; the fourfold assembly all harboring doubts symbolizes the excellence of the faculties and visions; and the manifestation of eighteen thousand lands.
The manifestation of these two [the earth and the drum] represents the excellence of responsive resonance; the sixfold trembling of the ground represents the excellence of supernatural powers;

the spontaneous sounding of the celestial drum and its preaching of the Dharma represent the excellence of preaching the Dharma; the joy of the great assembly of devas and nāgas represents the excellence of the retinue;

furthermore, seeing the various practices of the Buddha’s disciples represents the excellence of benefiting others. If one were to correlate these with the common environment (*sādhāraṇa-niśraya*), there are two [types].

If one holds the view that the suffering and happiness of a land depend upon sentient beings and are not created by the Buddha—the Buddha merely responding in accordance [with conditions]—then if he were to perform acts of subjugation or gathering-in, the Buddha would discern the karmic capacities and conditions to create either a land of suffering or a land of happiness; in this case, suffering and happiness would depend on the Buddha and not concern sentient beings.
This initial position is thus understood. If, however, one takes the meaning of subjugation and gathering-in, the Buddha does so through contemplation.

The various differentiations and coarse benefits found in other sutras are all included within the non-differentiated benefit of this sutra, or even further enter into its various wondrous benefits.
Alternatively, they may be categorized by position to demonstrate their wondrous benefits.
Regarding the benefits within the section on circulation: the practitioners who propagate [the teaching] encompass both ordinary beings and sages.
If Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body, adorned with vows, cause this land and other lands—whether lower or upper—to attain the seven provisional and real benefits, there are nine [categories].
The ten benefits further increase the merit of transformation, which returns to oneself to support the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), thereby increasing the Way and diminishing birth.

If a Bodhisattva of the birth-body (*janmakāya*) can likewise propagate the sutra in this land and other lands, enabling others to attain the provisional and the real—these seven benefits of transformation return to oneself to increase the Way and diminish birth—yet they cannot provide benefit in the higher lands. Even a teacher of ordinary persons can likewise propagate [the teaching] in this land.
By causing others to attain the seven benefits of the provisional and the ultimate, the merit of this transformative function returns to oneself, thereby increasing one’s own rank and level.

Regarding the methods for expounding the sutras, they are clearly set forth in the sacred words; the text states: "If sentient beings do not believe or accept [this], you should instruct, benefit, and gladden them by pointing toward other profound dharmas.
It further states: "Furthermore, employ diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting the primary meaning. These are the principles for propagating [the Dharma] in the present age.
Regarding the Dharma, whether one employs exclusively the Great [Vehicle] or exclusively the Small [Vehicle], neither captures the intent of the Buddha.

A skillful propagator of the sutras employs them according to the needs of the time; though their speech may express expedient means (*upāya*), their inner mind does not contradict the true Dharma (*dharmatā*).

Provided that sentient beings obtain the seven benefits of both the expedient and the real, the propagation of the sutra is fully realized. Furthermore, such circulation and benefit do not depend upon a third stage of circulation.

Duan Fangming has already pointed out within the main text itself that the benefits of propagating the sutra in the future are explained in the Parable Chapter, at the end of the Prophecy Chapter, and throughout the Dharma Master Chapter;
all of these clarify the merits and benefits of propagating the sutra.
Fourth, regarding the benefits observed within the mind: in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), it is taught that when the mind arises but has not yet moved the body or speech, it is not termed "karma.

In the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), however, it is taught that even a single *kṣaṇa* (instant) of committing a transgression results in calamity and a fall into the Avīci Hell. Avīci is a place of great suffering as retribution;

since the locus for initiating karma is as brief as a *kṣaṇa*, and the mind is so fleeting, how could heavy karma not be fully formed? How much more so, then, for the nine realms of existence (*navadhātu*) which are not yet complete?

If one can purify the mind, all karmas will be purified. Regarding the "contemplation of the pure mind," it means observing that all minds are dharmas produced by causes and conditions—immediately empty, immediately provisional, and immediately the Middle Way.
Through these three contemplations within a single mind, one knows that the mind is not the mind, for the mind is merely a name;
one knows that dharmas are not dharmas, for dharmas have no self; and one knows that names and namelessness are themselves the self.
Knowing that phenomena are non-phenomena is equivalent to Nirvana; when this understanding arises, the notions of "self" and "mine" are like clouds or illusions.
This is the benefit of the "cooling" [stage] on the Grounds. Furthermore, the arising of various wholesome states—such as faith, reverence, and a sense of shame—is the benefit of the cause.
To possess courage within the mind of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, corresponding moment by moment with emptiness itself, is the stage of "middle-sized grass and small trees."
The benefit of equality is that every thought-moment is conjoined with the provisional; the benefit of the great tree is that every thought-moment is conjoined with the middle;
the benefit of the most real matter is [conjoined with the real]. This concludes the fourth extensive explanation of the ten wonders.
Fifth, the conclusion regarding the provisional and the real: To illuminate the ten coarse realms is the provisional; to illuminate the ten subtle realms is the real.

As for the ten coarse [realms], they refer to the nine dharma-realms, the three causal conditions, and so forth—the various coarse truths and wisdoms, up to the coarse benefits—all of which are termed provisional.
To illuminate the ten subtle [realms] refers to the subtlety of principle, up to the subtlety of benefit; these are all termed subtle.

Therefore, for the sake of the reality, and furthermore for the sake of the ten marvels, the ten coarse [phenomena] are brought forth. Just as for the sake of the lotus, the intention lies in the lotus, yet the lotus remains hidden and does not appear;
so too, in other profound dharmas, there is instruction, guidance, benefit, and joy, and while other dharmas possess reality, that reality is not manifest.

As the text says: "The skillful means and the underlying intentions of the Tathāgata are difficult to understand. Furthermore, this is illustrated by the analogy of the flower opening and the lotus appearing.
To reveal the ten coarse [aspects] and manifest the ten subtle [aspects], there are no longer any coarse aspects; there is only the one Great Matter, an inconceivable realm, even unto its benefits.
If categorized according to the five flavors, the four *siddhāntas*, or the four gates, these are fully detailed in the complete volume.

One should know that although all teachings equally possess both the provisional and the real, the manner in which the provisional and real relate differs: some are exclusively real, some are exclusively provisional, and some are provisional...

Regarding the true aspect (*dharmatā*), both [the provisional and the real] are designated according to the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, yet their underlying principles have not yet been harmonized.

Now, judging by the teachings as a whole, the three vehicles of the *Tripitaka*, *Shared*, and *Distinct* teachings are provisional, while the Perfect Teaching (*Vimalakīrti*) is real. Furthermore, when the provisional and real aspects of the various teachings have not yet been harmonized, they are considered provisional;

once they are harmonized through the "opening of the provisional to reveal the real," they are considered real. Now, the *Lotus Sūtra* is this single Perfect Teaching and is therefore real; furthermore, it opens the provisional.

Therefore, it is called "real" (*satya*). If we speak from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), it illuminates the thirty coarse aspects of the three previous teachings as provisional (*upāya*) and illuminates the ten subtleties (*miao*) as real.
If we speak from the perspective of the perfect fusion that opens up the provisional, it determines that all thirty coarse aspects become subtle;

they are simply designated as "real," and for this reason they are called "subtle. If one takes the realization of principle (*li*) as the standard, then that principle is neither provisional nor real, for not even a single thing is seen [as separate].

The emptiness of dharmas is like an empty fist used to deceive a small child; to speak of the provisional and the real is considered a coarse principle, whereas that which is neither provisional nor real is therefore called "wondrous.

Second, regarding the explanation of the ten wondrousnesses based on the Root Chapter, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the root and the trace, and second, the explanation of the ten wondrousnesses. Explanation:

Regarding the distinction between the fundamental (hon) and the phenomenal (jaku), there are six aspects of the fundamental. First, the principle-fundamental is the true aspect (shōsō), which is the single ultimate path;
the phenomenal refers to everything other than the true aspect of all phenomena, all of which are termed "phenomenal.

Furthermore, both principle and phenomena are termed "fundamental," while the teaching that expounds principle and the teaching that expounds phenomena are both termed "phenomenal. Moreover, the teachings concerning both principle and phenomena are termed "fundamental," while practicing in accordance with those teachings is termed "phenomenal."
The traces of action are like a person who, by relying on a location, leaves footprints; by following the traces, one finds the location.

Furthermore, practice can realize the essence, and the essence serves as the fundamental basis; from the essence, function arises, and this function constitutes the trace. Moreover, that which is truly attained as essence and function is called the "fundamental," while that which is expediently manifested as essence and function is called the "trace.
This is explained in terms of what is revealed today as the fundamental and what was previously taught as the trace.
These six meanings clarify the relationship between the fundamental (ben) and the phenomenal (ji). First, clarifying the fundamental and the phenomenal in terms of principle (li) and phenomena (shi):
from the "root of non-abiding" (wuzhu ben), all dharmas are established. This principle of non-abiding is the true reality (shixiang zhendi) of the fundamental state;

all dharmas are the myriad phenomena (senluo susdi) of the fundamental state. From the true reality of the fundamental, one descends into the phenomenal traces; by investigating these phenomenal traces, one returns to the fundamental.
This reveals that although the fundamental and the manifested, the original and the trace, differ, they are inconceivably one; thus the text says:

"One contemplates all phenomena as empty, their true reality (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa), existing only through causes and conditions and arising from inversion. Regarding the clarification of the fundamental and the trace through both principle and teaching:
since the two truths illuminated at the time of the fundamental [enlightenment] are both ineffable, they are all termed the "fundamental" (*ben*). This was the Buddha’s skillful means of the past.
To speak of them is the teaching of the two truths; "teaching" (jiao) is termed the "trace" (ji). If there were no foundation of the two truths, there would be no two kinds of teaching.
Without the traces of teaching, how could the foundation of the truths be revealed? Although the foundation and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one.
A single passage states: "This Dharma cannot be shown; words and signs are quiescent. Yet, by the power of skillful means, [it is taught] for the sake of the five [classes of beings]."

When I speak of the threefold teaching of the provisional and the real as being based on practice, taking the original teachings received from the Buddha of the past as the "original" (hon), there arise the practices for cultivating causes and attaining fruits.
Through the teaching, the principle is expounded so that practice may be initiated; through practice, the teaching is realized so that the principle may be manifested.
Although the original and the manifest differ, they are inconceivably one. As a sutra says: "All dharmas, from the very beginning, are eternally..."

Since the Buddha-sons have practiced the path within the state of quiescent extinction, they shall attain Buddhahood in future ages. Fourth, regarding the names of essence and function as fundamental and trace:
because they originally attained the Dharma-body through their initial practice that accords with principle, this constitutes the "fundamental.

Because they give rise to the function of the Response-body from that very essence, and because the Dharma-body is manifested through the Response-body, there is the distinction between the fundamental and the trace. Although...
A particularly inconceivable passage states: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood, it has been exceedingly long ago;

yet, by means of skillful expedients (*upāya*), I have taught sentient beings by speaking in this manner. Fifth, regarding the clarification of the fundamental and the manifested through the provisional and the real:

the "real" refers to the original, remote past when he truly attained the Dharma-body and the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); both of these are termed the "fundamental. The intermediate periods, wherein he repeatedly proclaimed his births and deaths...
The various provisional teachings of the Dharma-response should both be called "traces" (jì) of the two bodies; they are not the original "Dharma-essence" (běn) of initial attainment.

Since there is no original essence, there can be no intermediate traces of the Dharma-response. It is through the traces that the essence is revealed. Although the essence and the traces differ, they are inconceivably one.
As a text says: "This is my skillful means; all Buddhas are likewise. Sixth, regarding the discussion of essence and traces from the perspective of the present, as mentioned previously:
All that has been taught in previous teachings—whether concerning phenomena or principle, or even the provisional and the real—is the "trace.
What is taught in this present sutra—concerning phenomena and principle from long ago, and even the provisional and the real—is called the "origin.

It is not that the origin from long ago, which is clarified here, was created to bestow upon the traces already taught; for how could the traces already taught manifest the present origin? Although the origin and the trace differ, [they are ultimately one].
A passage from the *Fahua yishu* states: "The Dharma of all Buddhas must, after a long period, speak the truth.

If one discusses the provisional and the real (*honjaku*) in terms of the past and the present, "the past" is designated as the provisional (*ke*), encompassing everything from Śākyamuni’s teaching at the site of enlightenment up to the ten coarse and ten subtle [teachings], all of which are termed the provisional.
"The present" is designated as the real (*hon*), collectively encompassing all the coarse and subtle teachings of the original time in the remote past.
If one speaks of "root" (*ben*) in terms of the provisional and the real (*quan-shi*), then pointing to the provisional as the "trace" (*ji*) subsumes all the various intermediate names;

the ten coarse and ten subtle aspects of the Buddha are all termed provisional, while pointing to the real as the "root" subsumes the initial ten coarse and ten subtle aspects, all of which are termed real.
If one speaks of "root" and "trace" in terms of essence (*ti*) and function (*yong*), then pointing to function as...

The "traces" (迹), which encompass the initial five wondrous aspects—namely, response and transformation (*nirmita*), supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), preaching the Dharma, retinue, and benefits—take the "essence" (体) as their fundamental basis, thereby encompassing the initial three wondrous aspects of the Dharma.

If one takes "practice" (行) as the basis for distinguishing between essence and traces according to the teachings, then practice is the trace, which encompasses the initial wondrous aspect of practice;

the "stage" (位) is the essence, which encompasses the initial wondrous aspect of the stage. If one takes "teaching" (教) as the basis for distinguishing between essence and traces, then the teaching is the trace, which encompasses the initial wondrous aspect of the time of the origin (本時).

If "wondrous wisdom" takes principle (*li*) and teaching (*jiao*) as the fundamental and the phenomenal (*ji*), then pointing to principle refers to the wondrousness of the fundamental realm attained at the beginning;
encompassing the teaching refers to the wondrousness of the teacher’s instruction attained at that time.

If both the fundamental teacher and the tenfold wondrousness are included, then if principle and phenomena (*shi*) are taken as the fundamental and the phenomenal, pointing to phenomena refers to the various coarse realms attained at the beginning, while pointing to principle refers to the fundamental.
In encompassing the various wondrous realms of the original time, the very first source is solely the fundamental (ben) and not the derivative (ji);
the final stage already explained is solely the derivative and not the fundamental; and the intermediate stages are both derivative and fundamental.

If there were no fundamental of the original time, it would be impossible to manifest the derivatives of the intermediate and final stages; if there were no derivatives already explained, it would be impossible to reveal those being explained now.
Although the origin and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one.
Second, to clarify the ten wonders of the origin: first, the wonder of the original cause; second, the wonder of the original fruit; third, the wonder of the original land;

fourth, the wonder of the original response and stimulus; fifth, the wonder of the original supernatural powers; sixth, the wonder of the original preaching of the Dharma; seventh, the wonder of the original retinue; eighth...
1. The Excellence of Original Nirvāṇa; 2. The Excellence of Original Life-span; 3. The Excellence of Original Benefit; 4. The Excellence of the Original Cause.
The "Excellence of the Original Cause" refers to the causes cultivated when first generating the bodhicitta and practicing the path of a bodhisattva.

For instance, when the sixteen princes propagated this sutra and formed karmic connections during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha, these were all deeds performed in the interim and not the original cause. They occurred after an incalculable number of kalpas had passed.

That which was practiced prior to the kalpa is called the "wondrous fundamental cause" (benyin miaoben), while the "wondrous fundamental fruit" (miaoben guo) refers to having attained ultimate permanence, bliss, self, and purity through the perfect and wondrous cause originally practiced; this is the fundamental fruit.

It does not mean taking Śākyamuni’s attainment of Buddhahood at the site of enlightenment as the fundamental fruit, but rather taking the initial realization since his attainment of Buddhahood—which has been for an exceedingly long time—as the fundamental fruit.
Regarding the fruit named the "Original Fruit" and the "Sublime Original Land": since the original fruit has already been realized, there must necessarily be a land upon which it relies.
Now, while the Trace [Buddha] resides in the Sahā world or among the three lands, there are also four lands in between. If so, the Original Buddha must also have a land;
where, then, does he reside? The text states: "From that time until now, I have constantly remained here in this Sahā world preaching the Dharma."
Regarding this text on transformation and instruction: it is truly not the Saha world within the traces of the present day, nor is it the provisional trace-locus of the intermediate period;
rather, it is the fundamental Saha, which is precisely the wondrousness of the original land.

Since the original responsive resonance has already achieved fruition, there exists the mutual correspondence between the capacity and the stimulus of the twenty-five kingly samādhis and the compassionate vows realized at the time of the origin.
Because the capacity of the barrier (*guan*) is such that it illuminates while being inherently quiescent, it is said to be "fundamentally responsive" (*ben ganying*).

As for "fundamental supernormal powers" (*ben shentong*), this refers to the previously attained meditative concentration of unmanifest transformation (*wujihua-hua chan*) combined with the various acts of compassion from the time of the original cause;

because these manifested transformations and supernormal powers startle and move the first beings to be converted, they are called "fundamental supernormal powers. As for "fundamental preaching of the Dharma" (*ben shuofa*), it is...

The Dharma taught by the fourfold eloquence when he first sat at the site of enlightenment, first attained perfect awakening, and first turned the wheel of Dharma in the past is called the "Original Teaching.
As for the "original retinue," these are the persons who were the recipients of the teaching at that original time;
those dwelling in the region below whom Maitreya does not recognize are precisely this original retinue. As for the "original nirvana," it refers to [the nirvana] at that original time...

The realization of the virtue of abandonment, which is *nirvāṇa*, likewise refers to the two lands—the Land of Shared Residence and the Land of Expedient Means—which were originally his appropriate dwelling places where he had karmic affinities.
Having delivered those with whom he was connected, he proclaims his entry into extinction; this is precisely his original *nirvāṇa*. Regarding his original lifespan:

since he proclaims his entry into extinction, there is the appearance of long or short, distant or near lifespans. Regarding his original benefit: it consists of the eight categories, including his original karma, vows, penetration, response, and so forth, along with his retinue.
This refers to the ten kinds of supreme benefits. These ten meanings are explained directly according to conditions and are scattered throughout the sutra texts;

however, they are now placed at the beginning as the fundamental causes, for it is necessarily through the cause that the fruit is attained. Because the fruit is accomplished, there is the land; because the fruit is perfected, there is the land.

Abiding in the land, there is the illumination of capacities; when capacities are moved, transformation is enacted; and when transformation is enacted, spiritual powers arise. Once spiritual powers are complete—[the following ensues].

Next, he preaches the Dharma; those who are reached by this preaching of the Dharma become his retinue. Once they have become his retinue, they are delivered, and their conditions being exhausted, they enter *nirvāṇa*.

Because of this *nirvāṇa*, one may discuss the length of their lifespan—whether long or short—and the benefits they perform, even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, including the benefits during the periods of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*).
These meanings are indeed immeasurable; yet, to summarize the beginning and the end, they are condensed into ten points of what is to be practiced and what is to be ceased.
This constitutes the sequence of accomplishment.

Regarding the identity and difference between the trace and the fundamental: within the trace, the cause is differentiated while the fruit is unified; by unifying the fruit of practice and the retributive fruit, they form the threefold wondrousness of the Dharma.

Within the fundamental, the cause is unified while the fruit is differentiated; by differentiating the fruit of practice and bringing forth the retributive fruit, the wondrousness of the fundamental land is clarified.

These similarities and differences are established according to the convenience of the meaning, with mutual inclusion and exclusion; the details within the traces are fully explained, while the original text concerning the stages of practice regarding object and wisdom is concise.
Generally summarized as the "Excellence of the Cause," it is understood that this opening and closing is merely a matter of perspective.

The "Excellence of the Fruit" is precisely the excellence of the three tracks (*trivartman*) within the traces; the names for response and resonance, supernatural powers, preaching the Dharma, and the retinue are all identical.

Regarding the opening of the supreme, fundamental, wondrous traces of *nirvāṇa* and lifespan—such as the Buddhas of the distant past, including Dīpaṃkara, Kāśyapa Buddha, and others—all of whom entered *nirvāṇa* within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
by inferring the underlying principle, it must be that these Buddhas were necessarily in a pure land for those with pure faculties, and because their past deeds were already accomplished.
As for why these two meanings (*nirvāṇa* and lifespan) do not appear among the wondrous traces [of Śākyamuni], although Śākyamuni...
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he proclaims *nirvāṇa* yet has not entered final extinction; this matter is precisely because he is currently within *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, the benefits are not distinguished within the provisional traces, as explained extensively above throughout this entire volume.

Regarding "coarse and subtle": within the provisional traces (*jì*), if one relies on the ten coarse aspects as coarse and the ten subtle aspects as subtle, this is based on what has not yet been revealed;

if one reveals the ten coarse aspects as coarse and reveals them as the ten subtle aspects, it is as fully explained previously. Within the traces, whether one relies on the coarse and subtle or reveals the coarse and subtle, this subtlety is no different from the fundamental subtlety (*běnmíào*).
Yet, it is said that [the former] is only now attained for the first time, whereas the latter was already established in the fundamental state. If [the former] is considered coarse...

Whether it be the subtle or the revelation of the coarse and the subtle, they do not differ. The trace is subtle because it is what was first attained; that which was first attained is designated as "subtle.

Furthermore, within the traces, the phenomena and principle are initially attained and thus considered "coarse," while within the source, the phenomena and principle were first attained and are thus considered "subtle.

The same applies to principle and teaching, teaching and practice, essence and function, and the provisional and the real. Moreover, for those who have not yet revealed the source by manifesting the trace, they understand only that which is within the trace.

The coarseness and subtlety of the phenomena and principles within the traces can ultimately never be understood; how much less so the phenomena-coarseness within the source, and even less so the principle-subtlety within the source.
Even Maitreya does not comprehend this, let alone others. If one awakens to the phenomena and principles within the traces, then the phenomena and principles within the source are revealed;
one also knows that it is by virtue of the phenomena and principles within the source that the phenomena and principles within the traces are manifested.

Since there is a fundamental principle, the fundamental is subtle while the derivative is coarse; because there is this distinction between the fundamental and the derivative, it is said that the coarse is subtle.

Yet, the wondrous principle is neither derivative nor fundamental—it is the inconceivable unity. The same applies to principle and teaching, teaching and practice, essence and function, the provisional and the real, the past and the present, and so forth.
Regarding the provisional and the real: that which illuminates the ten coarse realms within the traces is the provisional; that which illuminates the ten subtle realms within the traces is the real.
Furthermore, throughout the three periods of time, that which illuminates the ten coarse realms is the provisional, and that which illuminates the ten subtle realms is the real.
Whether provisional or real, they are all traces; because they are traces, they are called provisional. Thus, in the interim, they are immeasurable and...
The measure of the unspeakable is such that, among the provisional and the real, other sutras do not even possess one instance of the provisional in their midst, much less one instance of the real.
Since they lack even one instance of the provisional and real in their midst, how could they possess immeasurable instances?

Since they lack the provisional and real within the fundamental stage, all instances of the provisional and real in the intermediate stages are termed merely "provisional. From the very beginning, these illuminate the ten coarse levels.

The ten wonders are all termed the "Trace" (ji); the "Real" (shi) and the "Provisional" (quan), as well as the "Fundamental" (ben) and the "Trace" (ji), are all inconceivable. This inconceivability is itself the Dharma-nature (dharmatā).
The principle of Dharma-nature is neither ancient nor modern, neither fundamental nor traceable, neither provisional nor real;

it is only in relation to this Dharma-nature that we speak of the fundamental and the traceable, the provisional and the real, and the coarse and the subtle. Yet, by means of worldly words and letters, there are [distinctions of] past, future, and present.
It is not said that bodhi has past, future, or present. Furthermore, when distinguishing between the provisional and the real, there are three types:
namely, self-cultivation, transforming others, and both self-cultivation and transforming others, as explained in detail in the "Excellence of the Object" (*viṣaya-paramatā*) section.

Regarding self-cultivation, the two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—realized through one's own practice in the *Mūlabhūmi* (Original Ground) are called the Buddha’s own cultivation of the provisional and the real. From the primordial beginning until the Deer Park, these have manifested in various forms.

Through skillful means, he speaks according to the intentions of others; these two wisdoms of transformation revolve without fixed direction and are called the Buddha’s provisional and real wisdoms for transforming others.
Although there are two kinds of transforming others, both are termed "provisional"; although there are likewise two kinds of self-cultivation, both are termed "real.

This is what is meant by the combined explanation of the provisional and real regarding self-cultivation and transforming others. Furthermore, within the traces [of the teaching], the provisional is established based upon the real.

The intention lies in the real, yet that real intention is difficult to fathom. Why? Because the "transformed city" (the *pariṇāmika-nagara*) is a provisional means (*upāya*), yet people take it as real;

this is to fail to recognize the provisional and to be ignorant of the real. If one were to set aside the provisional to reveal the real, the intention would then reside in the provisional, and the provisional would be easy to fathom.

Why? Because once one knows that even a single matter such as the transformed city is a provisional bestowal by the Buddha, one will then universally penetrate all the Buddha-dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Because it universally penetrates the expedient means (*upāya*) of the distant past, the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that [the bodhisattva] is non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*); this is precisely the meaning of its frequent elucidation of numerical categories of phenomena.
As for "opening the provisional to reveal the real": once one has realized the phenomena of the provisional, the intent of the provisional ceases;

yet one does not depart from the provisional to seek the real afar. Since the provisional itself is the real, there is no longer a separate provisional—hence, it is said that "the provisional is opened to reveal the real."
Since the traces already contain these three meanings, such traces are manifested from the source; the source is likewise so.
Although the source and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one.

As for the contemplation of the mind, the source is wondrous, eternal, and far-reaching; how could it be that although the contemplation of the mind is not identical to the source, it is nonetheless not separate from the mind? How could this be?

The Buddha’s suchness and the suchness of sentient beings are one suchness, without duality. Since the Buddha has already contemplated the mind and attained this fundamental, wondrous trace of function—vast and beyond description—I, as a Tathāgata, must likewise contemplate the mind to bring forth this great benefit.
May my suchness quickly become the suchness of the Buddha. Therefore, the text says: "Upon hearing that the Buddha's lifespan is immeasurable, even for a brief moment, with a profound mind..."
Believing that his merit surpasses that [of others], may I, in the future, have long life to deliver sentient beings, just as the World-Honored One, the King among the Śākyas, now does;
may I, like him, fearlessly roar the lion’s roar at the site of enlightenment while preaching the Dharma.
May we, in the future, when sitting at the site of enlightenment and being honored by all, likewise preach such a long life. This is the contemplation of the mind.
This is the phase of the sixfold "immediate" attainment of the fundamental wondrous benefit.
Next, regarding the explanation of the "lotus": because the provisional and the real are difficult to manifest, the analogy of the lotus is borrowed to illustrate the Wondrous Dharma.

Furthermore, as there are many texts using seven metaphors, this is used as a title by way of analogy. Another interpretation states that the lotus is not merely a metaphor; it is named according to its own essence, similar to how an *kalpa* (aeon) is named.
In the beginning, all things were nameless; the Sage observed their principles and established names accordingly.

Just as a spider draws out silk to weave its web, or as one imitates the drifting of a tuft of grass to fashion a cart, or relies on floating logs to build a boat, or observes bird tracks to form written characters—all these are matters regulated by modeling them upon fundamental principles.
Thus, the designation "Lotus" is not a mere metaphorical fiction.
This is indeed the Dharma-gate of the Lotus; the Dharma-gate of the Lotus is the subtle and wondrous cause and effect of purity.
This Dharma-gate is "Lotus" (Padma) as the very essence of the Lotus Samādhi, not a mere metaphor.

In other sutras, the names are often explained by the texts themselves, yet this sutra lacks such an explanation; perhaps the text has not yet been transmitted [to us]. Nevertheless, both of these two explanations are well-founded.
The principle now harmonizes these two meanings: those of sharp faculties are said to "understand the principle" because they do not require metaphors, but merely apply the method of the Lotus Sūtra.

Those of middle and lower capacities have not yet awakened; they must rely on metaphors to know. Thus, the easily understood lotus flower is used as a metaphor for the difficult-to-understand lotus flower.

Therefore, there are three cycles of teaching to accommodate the upper, middle, and lower faculties. Regarding the upper faculty, it is a matter of the name of the Dharma; regarding the middle [faculty], it is a matter of the Dharma itself.

The preceding section was a metaphorical exposition discussing the three roots together, providing a dual heading for both the Dharma and its metaphors. For one who understands it in this way, with whom would there be dispute?
Since both the primary and secondary causes and effects are entirely the Dharma of the Lotus, what need is there for a metaphor to reveal them?

Nevertheless, because those of dull faculties do not understand that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is itself the Lotus, the worldly lotus is raised as a metaphor; how could this be considered an obstacle? However, the scriptural text contains two...
It is said that the udumbara flower appears but once in an aeon; if this flower blooms, a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) must appear.
When this sutra is preached, it is the bestowing of the prediction of Buddhahood (*vyākaraṇa*). Because this auspicious and miraculous flower resembles a lotus, it is used as a metaphor.

From this perspective, it is a metaphorical comparison (*upamā*) for the Sublime Dharma. Now, metaphors are of two kinds: partial metaphors and pervasive metaphors; for example, [the use of] the moon [as a metaphor].
It is like seeking eyebrows and eyes on a face; it is even more so than the Himalayas, for one cannot find its tail or tusks upon an elephant.

Now, regarding the Lotus Samādhi, there is nothing that can serve as a metaphor. Of all the various lotuses already mentioned, only this lotus—where both flower and fruit abound—is fit to serve as a metaphor.
This is because the cause contains the myriad practices and the fruit perfects the myriad virtues. Furthermore, other flowers...

The coarse metaphor refers to the causes and effects of the nine dharma-realms and the ten suchnesses; this flower serves as a subtle metaphor for the causes and effects of the Buddha-dharma realm and its ten suchnesses.
Furthermore, using this flower as a metaphor for the two gates of the trace and the source within the Buddha-dharma realm, each has three analogies.

Regarding the metaphor for the trace: first, when a flower blooms, there must be a lotus; it blooms for the sake of the lotus, yet the lotus itself cannot be seen. This analogy clarifies the provisional by means of the real.

The intention lies in the reality that there is no one capable of knowing it. Because the two flowers have opened, the lotus appears; yet, while the flower nurtures the lotus, this serves as a metaphor for how within the provisional there is the real, yet people cannot know it.

Now, the purpose of opening the provisional to reveal the real is so that one may extensively recognize the Buddha-dharma, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, solely for the sake of perfecting the Real and enabling a deep understanding of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. When the three flowers fall, the lotus is perfected.
This is illustrated by three metaphors: first, the discarding of the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle—the Single Buddha Vehicle—leading directly to the site of enlightenment;

second, that while Bodhisattvas who possess practice see it but not clearly, it is like flowers blooming; and third, that because the Buddhas do not [rely on] such practice, they see it with perfect clarity, just as when the petals fall and the lotus is formed.
These three metaphors illustrate how the "Trace Gate" (Jimon) leads from the initial skillful means into the Great Vehicle, reaching ultimate fulfillment.
Furthermore, there are three analogies for the Fundamental Gate (honmon): first, just as a flower must have a lotus, so too must the trace (jaku) have a fundamental basis;

while the trace contains the meaning of the fundamental, although it resides in the fundamental Buddha, his intent is difficult to know, and Maitreya does not recognize it. Second, just as when the flower opens the lotus appears, so too does the opening of the trace reveal the fundamental;
the intent lies in the trace itself being able to cause bodhisattvas to recognize the Buddha’s skillful means. Once the trace is recognized, one returns [to the fundamental].

Recognizing that the path increases and birth decreases at the source, the three metaphors of the falling petals and the lotus becoming full illustrate the abandonment of the traces to reveal the source.
Once the source is recognized, one no longer becomes confused by the traces; rather, one cultivates the path within the Dharma-body until it reaches fulfillment on the higher stages.

These three metaphors pertain to the beginning of the Root Gate, from its initial opening until its arrival at the stage of the original ground. Each of the six metaphors in these two gates has its specific correspondence, with the first set primarily concerning—

The ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm emerge from the ten suchnesses of the nine realms; next, by further opening up the ten suchnesses of the nine realms, the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm are revealed;

and finally, by threefold sublation of the ten suchnesses of the nine realms, the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm are perfected. These three analogies encompass the entirety of the beginning and end of the *Jiemo* (Trace) section.
If one grasps this meaning, then the twelve links of dependent origination, the four truths, the three truths, and so forth—along with their wisdoms, practices, and stages—[will all be understood].

The resulting merits and benefits are also illustrated by this same analogy. The fourth stage defines the ten suchnesses of the manifested Buddha-realm based on the ten suchnesses of the fundamental Buddha-realm;
the fifth stage reveals the ten suchnesses of the fundamental Buddha-realm by opening up the ten suchnesses of the manifested Buddha-realm;
and the sixth stage discards the ten suchnesses of the manifested Buddha-realm to establish the ten suchnesses of the fundamental Buddha-realm.
The ten realms, from their beginning to their end, are perfectly complete in their opening and closing; this constitutes a partial illustration by means of the lotus flower.
As for the extensive metaphor, it ranges from the initial seed to the formation of the lotus, serving as a simile for the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*).

For example, in a stone lotus, the black skin is on the outside and the white flesh is within; with the four subtle elements (*catvāraḥ paramāṇavaḥ*) as its substance, the rolled-up lotus bud is about to arise, containing within it a multitude of minute beings.
The opening buds, the spreading stamens, and the formation of the lotus seeds within the calyx—these remain unchanged from beginning to end.

This perfection of the ten meanings from the initial stage of the lotus to its final completion serves as a metaphor for the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) of the Buddha-realm and sentient beings, spanning from ignorance (*avidyā*) to the fruit of Buddhahood, without any deficiency.
[The general metaphor concludes: It is like a stone lotus; being black, it cannot be stained; being hard, it cannot be destroyed; being neither square nor... [text fragment ends].
Perfectly neither arising nor ceasing: because there was no seed at the beginning of the eon, it does not arise; because it is not different from that beginning, it does not cease.
This is called the characteristic of the lotus seed. The self-nature of the pure mind of all sentient beings is also like this:

though defiled by adventitious dust and burdened by the heavy accumulation of birth and death, the nature of the mind remains unmoving, unshakable, unarisen, and unceasing—this is precisely the Buddha.
The characteristics of the realms (*dhātu*) being thus pure, the meaning of "all sentient beings are the very aspect of Bodhi" is precisely this.
For example, although a lotus seed is within black husks and muddy soil, its white flesh does not change;

likewise, the wisdom that is the "enabling cause" (*laksanahetu*) for all sentient beings remains so even amidst the mud of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsa-sthāna*) and the karmic retributions of birth and death—their aspiration for omniscience remains as it is.
Because this nature is not lost even when it is designated as the "Buddha-realm," it is said that "afflictions are themselves bodhi.
Furthermore, the meaning of this is that while all phenomena are unarisen, prajñā arises. For example, although a lotus seed is within the mud, its four subtle elements do not decay;
this is called the essence of the lotus seed. The fundamental cause of Buddhahood (tathāgatagarbha) in all sentient beings is likewise always thus.
Bliss, self, purity, immovability, and indestructibility—these are called the Buddha-realm. Such is the greatness of its essence; as the Sūtra says:
"This flavor is true and correct, remaining steadfastly so that even mountains, grasses, trees, and thickets cannot cover or destroy it. This is precisely the meaning.
It is like a lotus seed, encased within its husk and submerged in mud, yet with its heart-core still curled and possessing the vital energy for growth.

The minds of all sentient beings are also like this: though bound by the fruits of suffering and submerged in the accumulation of delusions, they are able to give rise within them to the bodhicitta, which is exceedingly great, heroic, and fierce—like lion’s milk or a bowstring made of lion sinew.
This is called the power of the Buddha-realm. As the Sūtra says: "If one gives rise to the bodhicitta, it moves through boundless saṃsāra and shatters that which has no beginning."
There are people in Jambudvīpa who, though they have not yet seen the fruit, are able to courageously resolve their minds [for enlightenment].

For example, although a lotus seed is minute and small, within its black skin it already fully contains the roots, stems, flowers, petals, filaments, and anthers; all these components are present therein at once.
This is what is called a "lotus seed. In this same way, one should clearly understand that the initial generation of the bodhicitta by all sentient beings is likewise so.

Resolutely cultivating compassion and making vows to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below, vowing to attain accomplishment without ever wearying or retreating—this is called the Buddha-realm.
As the *Huashou jing* (Sutra of Mañjuśrī) says: "All merits and virtues reside within the initial mind. This is precisely that meaning.
It is like a lotus seed: its root depends upon the mud, yet its flower dwells in the void, swaying as it is touched by wind and illuminated by the sun.
Increasing in glory day and night, it provides all sentient beings with complete fulfillment;
it is likewise so for those who, from the limit of ignorance, give rise to the bodhicitta, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, and emerge from birth and death to enter into the dharma-nature.

Through the accomplishment of these practices, they encounter the Buddha-sun and are fanned by the wind of supernormal powers, such that their minds enter the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) in every thought-moment. This is called a Buddha.

Regarding the "elements" (*dhātu*) as such causes, the Sūtra states that the merit accumulated over immeasurable eons is not equal to the merit obtained from offering five lotus flowers to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
this refers to the meaning of the accomplishment of true causes.
For example, just as the filaments and anthers of a lotus flower surround it within the flower and outside the petals—this is called a "lotus"—so too are these conditions for the Bodhisattva.

It is likewise with the true cause (*hetu*): it is fully endowed with the myriad practices and the six *pāramitās*, such that one practice contains all practices, which assist the cause just as stamens exist within a flower.
When the fruit is attained, all manifold practices cease, just as the stamens are outside the lotus.
This is called the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*). Thus, the *Pratyaya-sūtra* says: "To exhaustively practice all the path-dharmas of the Buddhas..."
The meaning of this is as follows: it is like a lotus flower that has blossomed and formed a bud, while its petals fall away and the calyx matures into a fruit;
this is called the "lotus seed. In the same way, the Bodhisattva is likewise [like this]:

when the supreme *bodhi*, the great fruit induced by the true cause, is perfected and ultimately realized, this is called the "Buddha-realm" (*buddhadhātu*). Thus, the fruit is described in the sutra as: "O Son of the Buddha, practice..."

The meaning is that one who has already entered the Path shall attain Buddhahood in a future life. For example, just as the seed-cup and pericarp enclose the lotus seed—this is called a "lotus seed"—so too is the retribution of a Bodhisattva.
This great fruit is perfect and complete; it is the fruit of the fruit of the cultivated practice (*abhyāsa-phala*), which depends upon the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
Just as the stalk truly supports the pericarp, the Sūtra says: "Such a great fruit of retribution is attained through long cultivation."

That which is obtained through karma is precisely this meaning. It is like a clay lotus: the four subtle elements (*catvāraḥ paramāṇavaḥ*) of the lotus remain no different in their initial and final states while situated in space;

thus the lotus seed is called "equal from beginning to end. All sentient beings are likewise so: the four virtues (*catur-guṇa*) exist inherently at the beginning, yet being hidden they are termed the *tathāgatagarbha*;
when cultivated and perfected, these four virtues become manifest and are termed the *dharmakāya*. These inherent virtues and cultivated virtues are eternally blissful.
The purity of the self is one and non-dual; this is called the "Sutra on the Ultimate Equality of the Beginning and End of the Buddha-realm.
The statement that "the suchness of sentient beings is the same as the suchness of the Buddha, being a single suchness without duality" is precisely its meaning.

Having thus used the lotus to illustrate the ten aspects of suchness (*daśatathatā*), next the lotus is used to illustrate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*): the black skin, the mud, the water, and the layers of grass covering it are these very [links].

The power of the seed of the limb of ignorance (*avidyā*) to produce is itself the limb of formations (*saṃskāra*); its internal possession of the coiled lotus filaments is the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna*);
its containing moisture is the limbs of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*);

its being a compact, coiled mass from which it cannot emerge is the limbs of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*); and its ability for the tip of the sprout to stir and pierce through the rind is the limb of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
The extinction of ignorance such that it no longer remains within the bird's skin represents the extinction of *saṃskāras*; emerging from the eggshell represents the extinction of old age and death.

This is a brief analogy for the fourfold twelve-linked chain of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). To illustrate the Four Noble Truths: the bird's skin represents suffering within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*);

the white flesh represents the origin (*samudaya*) within the realm of desire; the mud represents the origin outside the realm of desire; and the water represents suffering outside the realm of desire.
The path and cessation can be known; this collectively illustrates the fourfold Four Noble Truths. To illustrate the Two Truths:

the lotus, its fibers, stem, and leaves represent the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the hollows within the lotus, fibers, stem, and leaves represent the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); this collectively illustrates the sevenfold Two Truths. To illustrate the Three Truths:

the ultimate and conventional truths are as previously described, while the four subtle elements (*mahābhūta*) correspond to permanence, bliss, self, and purity, representing the Middle Way, the Truth of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-satya*).
This passage generally illustrates five kinds of the three truths: the non-arising and non-ceasing of the four subtle elements illustrate the one ultimate truth;

the non-arising at the beginning of the kalpa and the non-ceasing at the present time illustrate the truth of no-truth and no-explanation. The use of the lotus flower to illustrate the wondrousness of the object is thus concluded.

Next, regarding the analogy of the nine wonders: the internal generative nature is analogous to the wonder of wisdom (prajñā); the stalk and generative nature are analogous to the wonder of the wisdom of emptiness (śūnyatā-jñāna);

the filaments and leaves and their generative nature are analogous to the wonder of the wisdom of the provisional (upāya-jñāna); and the four subtle elements of the lotus pedestal and their generative nature are analogous to the wonder of the wisdom of the Middle Way (madhyama-jñāna).

These three analogies for the generative nature illustrate the wonder of the three wisdoms within one mind. Although the lotus seed is small, it fully possesses the root, stem, leaves, and flower; this is analogous to practice (caryā).
The wondrous stem is wisdom; the leaves are compassion; the filaments are samādhi; and their full blossoming is liberation.

Furthermore, the leaves are likened to the three types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*): the blue leaves covering the water represent the compassion based on conditions (*parigraha-maitrī*); the yellow leaves covering the water represent the compassion based on dharmas (*dharmālambana-maitrī*);

and the leaning leaves represent the unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*). If the lotus emerges from the leaning leaves, it will not long before it blooms; when unconditioned compassion is perfected, one receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

Before long, the roots, stems, seeds, and leaves benefit people; the bees represent *dāna* (generosity), the fragrance represents *śīla* (ethical discipline), the mud-born growth represents *kṣānti* (patience), the increase represents *vīrya* (diligence), the soft moisture represents *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), and the lack of defilement represents *prajñā* (wisdom).
These serve as metaphors for the excellence of practice (*caryā*). The lotus serves as a metaphor for principle (*tattva*), representing the stages (*bhūmi*).

The sprout piercing the outer skin represents the stage of coarse abiding (*sthiti*), while the sprout emerging from the skin represents the stage of subtle abiding. Piercing [the inner layers] represents the stage of penetration.

The stage of mud represents the level where desire is still present; emerging from the mud but not yet reaching the water represents the four dhyānas (the stage of meditative concentration), which, like water, can wash away the dust of desire.
Being situated in the water and growing represents the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). This analogy extends up to this point.

The lotus of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) represents the stage of breaking through both afflictions of views and afflictions of thought (*darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya*). Emerging above the water represents the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), where the lotus is contained within the air and is about to blossom.
The stamens and pedestal being recognizable symbolizes the stage of the Ten Abidings; opening and turning in accordance with the sun symbolizes the stage of the Ten Practices;

unfolding and achieving maturity while bearing the weight [of the world] like bees and butterflies symbolizes the stage of the Ten Dedications; the stamens and petals falling away while the lotus seed remains alone symbolizes the stage of resting from all practices;
and the ultimate fruit of wondrous enlightenment, being without affairs, truly eternal, and profoundly tranquil, symbolizes the stage of fruition—all of these are metaphors for the stages.

The lotus is subtle; it possesses four subtle elements (*aṇu*) which illustrate the track of true nature (*dharmatā-niyāma*). The hollowness within the lotus pod and the hollow stalks of the filaments illustrate the track of contemplative observation (*avalokana-niyāma*).
The surrounding arrangement of the petals and the pod illustrates the track of supportive accomplishment (*parigraha-niyāma*). This analogy illustrates the subtlety of the threefold Dharma-vehicle.

When the lotus forms in empty space, its reflection appears in clear water, illustrating the manifest capacity and the manifest response. When the reflection appears in turbid water, it illustrates the hidden capacity and the hidden response. The shadow [of the reflection] is the response.

The analogy of tree shadows on water in the wind is both obscure and manifest; as the *Dafangdeng Dajing* (Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra) states, "The shadow of a tree in the dark, its reflection appearing in the water at night," this is neither obscure nor manifest.
Such analogies illustrate the wondrous nature of the response to stimuli (*ganying*).

If a lotus flower is shaken by the wind, tilting eastward and falling westward, reflecting southward and sinking northward—closing when the wind blows downward and opening when the wind blows upward—this is precisely...
The analogy of the east rising while the west sinks, and the center rising while the periphery sinks, illustrates the omen of the earth-trembling.

The closing of the flowers at dusk illustrates the omen of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The opening of the flowers at sunrise illustrates the omen of preaching the Dharma. Viewing from afar they appear red, while viewing from nearby they appear white;

the red flowers and green leaves reflecting one another in brilliant splendor illustrate the omen of emitting light. The pervasive fragrance throughout the fields illustrates the omen of the sandalwood breeze.

The drifting medicinal powder is like the auspicious celestial flowers; the scattering raindrops that turn into pearl-like clusters are like the auspicious self-resounding celestial drums—all these serve as metaphors for the wondrousness of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The closed flowers not yet blooming represent the concealment of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) while teaching the three vehicles separately;

the flowers and petals fully blossoming represent the convergence of the three back into the one through the teaching of the One Vehicle alone; and the falling of the petals while the lotus remains represents [the ultimate reality].
To transcend teachings and penetrate the profound principle—knowing that the Tathāgata never speaks the Dharma—is what is called "much learning. These examples illustrate the subtlety of the Dharma.
From one lotus stalk, another flower grows; from that, in turn, immeasurable lotuses are produced, illustrating the subtlety of karma producing a retinue.
From the seed-pod of a lotus, seeds fall into the mud and grow into lotuses again, which in turn produce more.
The immeasurable lotuses are like the excellence of the retinue of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*);

those [lotuses] from the *Mudgala* pond are gathered and their seeds planted in this pond, where the lotuses flourish, which is like the excellence of the retinue of those who aspire to be born [there].

Those [beings] flying from that pond are like drifting silk-filaments and thin mists entering this pond where the lotuses flourish, which is like the excellence of the retinue of those who are born there by necessity. Fish and turtles gasp and pant therein...

Below, bees and butterflies flock and alight upon it; this is like the wondrous benefit of the coolness of sentient beings' karmic fruition, by which those who see it rejoice—this is like the benefit of the cause.
To gather its leaves is like the benefit of the three types of grasses; to gather its flowers is like the benefit of the wondrous small trees;
to gather its lotuses is like the benefit of the wondrous great trees; and to gather its filaments is like the benefit of the wondrous reality of the fruit.
These analogies for the excellence of merit and benefit have been explained; next, the analogy for the fundamental nature is as follows:
Suppose there is a pond where lotuses first ripen, and having ripened, they fall into the mud and water, only then to grow again until they reach maturity.

In this manner, through repeated cycles, they continue to grow and ripen over the passage of years and months, until they eventually fill the entire great pond and its flower fields. The Buddha is also like this.

Having already completed the cultivation of the causal practices and the realization of the fruit from the very beginning, for the sake of sentient beings, he further gives rise to skillful means within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

He manifests the initial arousal of the bodhicitta and again demonstrates the ultimate attainment. Through countless hundreds of thousands of repeated births and deaths, he descends to manifest his response in accordance with ordinary people, further cultivating the five practices.
The lotus flower growing again from its stem and leaves serves as a metaphor for further cultivating the four noble practices.
Increasing ever so slightly, it is like further cultivating the practice of the heavens; the initial growth of a lotus leaf is like further cultivating the Brahma-practice;

the falling of a lotus seed into the mud is like joining with all evils while further cultivating the practice of illness; and the initial sprouting of a lotus bud is like joining with minor virtues while further cultivating the infant-practice.
Thus, the benefit to sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is beyond measure, pervading the entire Dharma-realm without exception.

The emanation of bodies and the manifestation of traces—whether through hearing the traces or abandoning the traces—provide equal benefit; were it not for the lotus flower, by what means could these be universally illustrated?
Since the preceding dharmas have been explained through the dual analysis of both principle and parable, it is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Sublime Dharma).
Next, to explain the general name [of this scripture], it consists of the single character "Jing" (經). In Sanskrit, it is called *saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
*Saddharma* is translated as "Sublime Dharma" (*miaofa* 妙法), and *puṇḍarīka* is translated as "Lotus" (*lianhua* 蓮華), as has already been explained above.

*Sūtra* is also referred to as *sūdanra* or *sutulu*; these are regional dialects of that land (India), just as there are differences between the "Chu" and "Xia" dialects here in China. Thus, the translations vary according to the local vernaculars.

Regarding the terms "without equivalent" (*wúfán*) or "with equivalent" (*yǒufán*), there are five explanations: first, clarifying those without equivalent; second, clarifying those with equivalent; third, harmonizing existence and non-existence;
fourth, applying this to all phenomena to clarify the sūtra; and fifth, contemplating the mind to clarify the sūtra.

Regarding the term "wúfān" (no equivalent): that [Sanskrit] language contains many meanings, whereas this [Chinese] language is single and shallow; thus, it is impossible to translate the complex with the simple, and one should instead retain the original sound.
As for the term "jīng" (sūtra), Kāiśàn said: "It is not a direct translation, but merely using this word here to represent that one there.

In this land, what the sages speak is called "jīng," while what the worthies speak is called "zǐshǐ" (biographies and histories). Since the sages of that [other] land call it "jīng" and Bodhisattvas call it "lùn" (treatise), it cannot [be so translated].

Rather, it is precisely because this [term] can serve as a substitute for that [Sanskrit term] that it is called "sūtra" (*jing*), which encompasses five meanings: first, the source of the Dharma (*dharmamūla*);
second, subtle manifestation (*sūkṣmaprakāśana*); third, a gushing spring; fourth, a carpenter’s line; and fifth, a string of garlands.

Now, we shall simply treat these as five meanings and not attempt to translate them into three within the single category, nor expand them into fifteen by tripling the five. Regarding the first meaning, "the source of the Dharma": one...
All things are ultimately inexpressible; yet, by means of the four *siddhāntas*, there is verbal expression. According to the *loka-siddhānta*, speech serves as the foundation for teaching.

According to the *puruṣa-pratipakṣa-siddhānta*, it serves as the foundation for practice. According to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, it serves as the foundation for meaning. Regarding the foundation of verbal teaching:
that which is spoken from the Golden Mouth takes a single word as its root, from which an immeasurable array of teachings branches forth. If...

If the Way were separate from the time it was heard by beings, they would have attained the Way immediately; therefore, the Sūtra says that each and every sūtra has immeasurable sūtras as its retinue.

If later generations do not understand, the Bodhisattva takes the Buddha’s teachings as the basis to compose general treatises and specific treatises, expounding upon both general and specific sūtras so that the Buddha’s intent is not obstructed, and those who seek it may attain the Way.
This is truly because this treatise has its foundation. Although the various non-Buddhists have their own doctrines, they do not accord with the Sūtras;
being based on mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) without a foundation, they cannot attain the Way. The Sūtra is the foundation of practice:

it shows people the Dharma of non-contention, guides them through obstacles and openings, clarifies the eyes, and heals the maladies of humanity. If one practices according to the teaching, then both common and extraordinary powers will arise.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) proceed from here to there, entering the cool pond and reaching the stage of ambrosia (*amṛta*), the true Dharma-treasure of *nirvāṇa*.
Because sentient beings enter through various gates, one knows that the sūtra is the root of practice and the sūtra is the root of meaning.

Thus, by investigating a single phrase, one realizes a single meaning; by investigating immeasurable phrases, one realizes immeasurable meanings; or, by investigating a single phrase, one realizes immeasurable meanings.

One investigates infinite phrases that express a single meaning, whether in their general or specific aspects; because one investigates these expressions to penetrate and enter [the meaning], the sūtra is the basis for this meaning.

When these three types are bound together as "Dharma-gates," the basis of the teaching is *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing), the basis of practice is *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection), and the basis of meaning is *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation).
Since the meaning of the basis of the true Dharma already contains many layers of implication, it cannot be translated [into a single term].

Furthermore, some say that the arising [of the teaching] may be understood by analogy with this. Moreover, when the teaching is subtle, the practice is subtle; when the meaning is subtle, the teaching is a gushing spring;

when the practice is a gushing spring, the meaning is a gushing spring; when the teaching is like a carpenter’s line, the practice is like a carpenter’s line; when the meaning is like a carpenter’s line, the teaching is like a garland;

when the practice is like a garland, the meaning is like a garland; and so as to prevent them from falling into ruin. All these details are as found in the complete volume. Furthermore, regarding the *sūtra*...
