some see the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) in the Lotus Treasury World-Ocean preaching the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground to billions of Śākyamuni Buddhas; or they see the Dharma Body (dharmakāya).
It is identical to empty space—without discrimination, without marks, and without obstruction—pervading equally throughout the Dharma-realm.

One may see this place as mountains, forests, earth, soil, or sand; one may see it as the seven treasures; or one may see this place as the locus where all Buddhas of the three periods of time have practiced;
or one may see this place as the true realm of the inconceivable Buddhas.
The Dharma is like the sun: when it first rises, it first illuminates the high mountains; when it is about to set, its lingering radiance should likewise reach the lofty peaks.
Thus, the Lotus Treasury Ocean extends even to after the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, let alone to the preceding teachings.

Regarding the Sūtra as the "half-curd" teaching, if discussed separately, it belongs to the second period; yet if discussed generally, it also reaches the latter [period]. The Commentary states: "From the initial Deer Park..."
One should know that the precepts, concentration, and wisdom taught by the Buddha at Venuvana until the night of his parinirvāṇa were compiled as the *Sūtra* and other Piṭakas;

thus, the Three Piṭakas generally extend to the later period. If one discusses them specifically in relation to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (the "Half" and "Full" teachings) and the *Prajñāpāramitā* (the "Butter" teaching), this is the third period;
however, in general terms, it also extends to the later period. Regarding the *Dhāraṇī*, it says: "First, in Rājagṛha, he bestowed [teachings] upon the Śrāvakas."
The record states that he has now again bestowed predictions upon the śrāvakas in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī;

therefore, we know that the Vaipulya [sūtras] extend through to after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*, if discussed specifically, it is a teaching of "half" that brings the "full" to maturity, belonging to the fourth period.

However, if discussed generally, it extends from the beginning to the end. Why? Because from the night of his attainment of the Way until the night of his parinirvāṇa, he constantly preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* as the "cream of the cream" (*sarpir-maṇḍa*), if one discusses it according to the distinct periods of the teaching, it belongs to the fifth period; yet, if discussed according to the general teaching, it also reaches back to the beginning. The *Śāstra* states:

"From the first generation of the mind of awakening, one constantly contemplates *nirvāṇa* while practicing the path. Does this not imply that in the various preceding teachings there were no bodhisattvas who generated the mind and contemplated *nirvāṇa*?
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "When I sat at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, I first attained perfect awakening."
At that time, bodhisattvas from immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges had also once questioned me regarding this profound meaning;
the phrasing and meaning of their questions were likewise identical to these, without any difference. Those who ask in such a manner can benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
This point connects back to what was previously discussed in terms of the explicit teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Because there is no obstruction to the principles of the *Guhyaka-paryāya* (the *Guhyakasamāja-tantra*) as it is not seen to be prior [to this teaching], Śāriputra said:

"In the past, I heard such a Dharma from the Buddha, wherein I saw various bodhisattvas receiving predictions of their attainment of Buddhahood. Is this not a scriptural passage that serves as evidence for the universal prediction (*sāmānya-vyākaraṇa*)?
Regarding the recorders' private notes, it is said: "Some say that during the second period, for twelve years, the distinct teachings of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*) were expounded. If...
If twelve years have passed and there are those who ought to hear the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections, how can you say they should not be taught?
If they are taught, then the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles would not be restricted to these twelve years;

yet if they are not taught, how could the Buddha fail to transform those who are present later and ought to hear them? Certainly, such a principle does not exist. When the Sūtra says "for the sake of the Śrāvakas," it means this.
The teaching of the Four Truths up to the Six Perfections did not cease for twelve years; rather, throughout his entire lifetime, he taught whatever was appropriate for those who heard him.
This is evidenced by the *Catur-āgama* and the five divisions of the Vinaya, which were taught for the sake of the Śrāvakas until the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa—this is precisely what that means.
How can one claim that the Hīnayāna teachings were completed within twelve years? Some people say... [text ends]

Regarding the statement that the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Saṃdhinirmocana* occurred during the three periods within thirty years: on what scriptural passage does one rely to know it was thirty years?

As for the forty years, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that after forty years had passed since the Buddha attained enlightenment, Maitreya says, "Since the Buddha attained the Way, only slightly more than forty years have elapsed.
However, one cannot say that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is definitively situated [at the end of] the forty-year period.

Regarding the question at the end of this chapter: Why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* state that Subhūti heard in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that even those who merely raise their hands or bow their heads shall all attain Buddhahood, and thus now inquires about the meaning of "retrogression"? If that were so, how could the sequence between the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* be fixed?
However, as for the relative depth and shallowness of the three teachings—the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Nirvāṇa*—it is difficult to speak of them rashly.

What is this? Nirvana, Buddha-nature, Prajñā, and the One Vehicle are all one and the same. The One Vehicle is the core tenet of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while Prajñā is that which is expounded in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
it is precisely the elucidation of this nature. Furthermore, what remains unclarified?

The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* speaks of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), which is no different from the emptiness clarified in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Both state that "form is empty," and so forth.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra also states that [Nirvana] is empty, while the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra says that Nirvana is not an illusory transformation;
the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra speaks of the Buddha-body as being free from the five kinds of impermanence, clarifying its permanence and stating that Nirvana is not empty.

What difference is there [between these], such that you yourself give rise to the distinction that the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa exclusively emphasizes and clarifies permanence, while the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra speaks solely of emptiness? Furthermore, if one follows the Lotus Sūtra...
Regarding those who enter *nirvāṇa*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already clarified that the royal palace was not the beginning;
having attained enlightenment long ago, why would one only now cite the initial attainment under the Bodhi tree as a basis for doubt by clinging to it as real?

Thus we know that this refers to a class of sentient beings who hear the teaching of the Eternal (*nitya*) for the last time. Those who have heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* do not need to hear the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; furthermore, it should be...
One should know that the ultimate aim of all Mahāyāna sūtras is no different; they differ only according to what is appropriate for the occasion.

For example, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* all take samādhi as their title; Prajñā is great wisdom; the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* speaks of inconceivable liberation, which is liberation;
Great Nirvāṇa is ultimate cessation; and the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta* is the fulfillment of the path.
All these are the Buddha-dharma; in the Dharma there is no superiority or inferiority. Among them, what is clarified as the fruit is entirely the Buddha-fruit;

what is clarified as the cause is entirely the practice of the stages (*bhūmi*); and what is clarified as the principle is entirely the *dharmatā*. That which is enacted is the ultimate destination of the Bodhisattvas, and it ought not to differ.
Why then do people insist on creating distinctions of superiority and inferiority? Nevertheless, according to the sūtras and śāstras, there are briefly two types: namely, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
And as for the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, its teaching is necessarily directed toward individuals, with two distinct types for each.

Within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka, there are those who are fixed as śrāvakas and those who have regressed from the bodhicitta. Within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, there are great beings of sudden enlightenment and those who enter gradually.
Among the fixed śrāvakas, some remain solely in the Lesser Vehicle, while others who have regressed in mind may later be able to proceed toward the Great Vehicle. Although...
Because there are those who depart and those who remain, yet they are identical in their reception of the Small [Vehicle], what is taught for these two types of persons is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
Although Bodhisattvas differ in being either sudden or gradual, they are identical in their reception of the Great [Vehicle];

therefore, what is taught for these two types of persons is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Furthermore, these two piṭakas correspond to their respective purposes and their respective teachings; within the Śrāvaka-piṭaka...
The Bodhisattvas act as its shadow and echo, yet it is not their primary purpose; one must not follow them [in this regard].
Among the Mahāyāna sūtras within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, there are also śrāvakas, but they are not the primary focus of the doctrine, for the teachings of the śrāvakas are not expounded therein.
Therefore, it cannot be called a Hīnayāna dharma. When comparing persons and defining dharmas, each is distinct; thus, one must summarize and encompass them accordingly.

Briefly, there are only two; now, by opening and dividing them, they are judged as four teachings: the Śrāvaka-piṭaka corresponds to the Tripiṭaka Teaching; the Bodhisattva-piṭaka corresponds to the Shared, Distinct, and Complete Teachings.
The Tripiṭaka Teaching is taught for those who are determined Śrāvakas; the Shared Teaching is taught for those Great Śrāvakas who may regress;
the Distinct Teaching is taught for Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment; and the Complete Teaching is taught for Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment.
It is not merely that names and numbers are easy to harmonize while meanings and intentions are profoundly unified; rather, the seals of past and present coincide as one without duality.

Yet, while the texts are concise, the meanings are vast; the teaching is singular, yet it encompasses all. If one were to unfold the hidden to make it manifest, one must extensively compose treatises and commentaries—much like setting traps and nets in rivers and marshes when hunting.
Is it that the fisherman or the hunter delights in such abundance? It is simply unavoidable.
This is merely a broad overview.
*The Essential Summary of the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra*, Volume Lower:
Epilogue to the Essential Summary of the Profound Meaning.
The Dharma-gate of a single word could not be fully recorded even with ink as vast as the ocean; how then can the wondrous discourse of ninety days be said to be exhaustive?
Furthermore, even if one were to employ the four types of eloquence throughout those ninety days to proclaim its literary meanings, they would be limitless.

What Chanzhang has recorded is already quite abbreviated; how could it be further edited or condensed? It is only because those of dull faculties in this degenerate age fear complexity and delight in brevity.
Gazing toward the wondrous and profound [teachings] as if they were a vast ocean, the "sweet-frog" remains there, guarding its position and refusing to advance;
thus, throughout their entire lives, they fail to receive even a single drop of the unsurpassed *amṛta* (clarified butter). This is truly lamentable.
I have heard that while Kumārajīva reduced the thousand fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by tenfold, Jingxi [Zhiyi] likewise recorded the essential meaning of the entire *Mohe zhiguan*.

Therefore, I have modeled myself after his intent and compiled these *Jieyao* (Essential Excerpts) in two fascicles, hoping that [the reader] might more easily "dip a finger" [into the flavor] and gradually become replete with the taste of the Dharma.

Only then, by extensively investigating the profound texts and deeply realizing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, will this undertaking perhaps not fail to be one method of gradual and skillful guidance.
As for those who, however, cling to these essential excerpts as sufficient unto themselves and ultimately...
If one leaves the profound texts unexplored, I am certainly a sinner against the wise Master Zhiyan, and he, in turn, is a sinner against me.
On the twenty-sixth day of the second month of summer in the Gengchen year, Zhixu respectfully records this.
